en: Commentary on the Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the Protection of the State, Scroll One:
Introduction, Chapter One: The Prologue.
Spoken by the Great Master Tiantai Zhizhe; recorded by his disciple Guanding.
The Great Master, following a standard precedent in various sutras, establishes fivefold profound meanings (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*):

first, the explanation of names (*nāma-nirukti*); second, the discernment of the essence (*tattva-viniścaya*); third, the clarification of the core principle (*mūla-prayojana*); fourth, the discussion of its function (*vṛtti-karma*); and fifth, the classification of the teaching (*śāsana-vibhāga*).

This sutra takes person and dharma as its title, the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its essence, the causes and effects of one’s own practice as its thesis, the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real as its function, and the "ripened butter" of the Mahāyāna as its pedagogical characteristic.
Regarding what is called the "title," there are both general and specific aspects.
The single character "sūtra" (經) applies generally to all sections.
The phrase "The Buddha’s Teaching on the Benevolent Kings’ Protection of the Nation Prajñāpāramitā" is the specific title.
Furthermore, the *Benevolent Kings’ Sūtra on Protecting the State* (*Renwang Huguo*) spoken by the Buddha refers specifically to this particular section,
whereas the *Prajñāpāramitā* refers to the entire collection of sections.
Moreover, the *Benevolent Kings’ Sūtra on the Prajñāpāramitā for Protecting the State* spoken by the Buddha is the general title for this entire work.
The first chapter, "Introduction," is a specific title within this collection.
However, the titles established for various sutras differ: some refer solely to the Dharma, such as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*;
others refer solely to the person, such as the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
Some titles derive solely from a metaphor, such as the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*;
some employ both a person and a dharma, such as the *Vimalakīrti* and this present sūtra;
and some cite both a dharma and a metaphor, such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Alternatively, there are three kinds of perfection, as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

That which is called "Buddha" carries the meaning of being endowed with virtue: self-awakening distinguishes him from ordinary beings; awakening others distinguishes him from [lesser] sages; and the fulfillment of awakening distinguishes him from bodhisattvas.
The eight musical tones being proclaimed and flowing forth is called "preaching";
this refers to the person who preaches.
The phrase "Benevolent Kings" (*Renwang*) below clarifies the Dharma that is preached.
One who bestows grace and spreads virtue is called "benevolent" (ren), and one who governs with sovereign mastery is termed a "king" (wang).
A benevolent king is the protector, while the realm is that which is protected; this is because the benevolent king governs the country through the Way.
If one regards *prajñā*, then *prajñā* is that which protects and the Benevolent King is that which is protected; because he upholds *prajñā*, the Benevolent King is secure and at ease.
If, however, it is the king who is able to transmit the Dharma, then the king is that which protects and *prajñā* is that which is protected.

Furthermore, "benevolence" (ren) means patience (kṣānti). Upon hearing of good, one does not immediately rejoice; upon hearing of evil, one does not immediately become angry. Because one is able to harbor and endure both good and evil, it is called patience.
The "Ruler" (wang) signifies governance; it is because the four quarters submit to his governance.
This is an explanation based on causes and conditions (*nidāna*).
According to the provisional teaching (*yijiao*), one perceives the arising of all phenomena and knows that this arising is real.
Seeing that all phenomena are extinguished, extinction is emptiness; because emptiness is unmoving and unchanging, the six sense objects and the realms of existence remain as they are.
When the fetters of the three realms are exhausted, the King is secure and at peace; what is attained by these two vehicles is called the "Benevolent Kings."
This is the intent of the Tripiṭaka.

To attain mastery within the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages—wherein one contemplates that the form of all dharmas is itself emptiness, neither arising nor ceasing, like an illusion or a transformation—and thereby suddenly and simultaneously severing the afflictions of the triple world to dwell within the "Transformation City" beyond the realms; therein, giving rise to the thought that one has already crossed over and the thought of peace and security, such are the practitioners of the Three Vehicles who together traverse the Ten Stages. They are able to protect the kingdom of the Transformation City with its remaining skillful means, each attaining the title of King.
This is the intent of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).

If one contemplates that all phenomena are empty and that this emptiness is itself form (*rūpa*), then because form is boundless, the *prajñāpāramitā* and other dharmas are likewise boundless. Although they are boundless, they do not obstruct the mind, just as when a box is large, its lid is also large.

Yet the boundless Dharma resides within a single mind; within each and every phenomenon, all Buddha-dharmas are fully present. From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one attains perfection stage by stage and dwells upon the lotus pedestal. Being unmoving and unchanging, yet capable of moving and transforming, this is the state of the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, who each preside as kings over the six perfections, such as generosity (*dāna*).
This is the intent of the Separate Teaching (*prthaktīya*).

If one contemplates that all phenomena are originally unarisen and thus now non-extinguished—such that although there is no arising or extinction, arising and extinction are nonetheless manifest—one simultaneously illuminates both and simultaneously transcends both, thereby accords with the Middle Way. Vast as the Dharma-realm and ultimate as empty space, from the first stage (*ādikṣānti*) up to the Buddha-stage, one clearly and distinctly realizes the principle of the Middle Way through the forty-two minds; abiding in the light of eternal quiescence, each attains the title of King.
This is the intent of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

Furthermore, within the Tripitaka (Sanzang), Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are called "Benevolent Kings" (Renwang) because they have exhausted their afflictions; however, Bodhisattvas and those on the stages of fruition or the path of patience (*kṣānti*) have not yet exhausted their views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*), and thus they are called only "Kings," not "Benevolent. In the Buddha-ground of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), the Subtle Enlightenment of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), and the ultimate fruit of the Perfect Teaching, each is a "Benevolent King."
The teachings themselves possess degrees of superiority and inferiority; if it is not the Benevolent King of the Three Teachings, then it is the [Benevolent King] of the One Vehicle.

If we consider them in terms of the provisional and the fundamental, the Benevolent Kings of the three teachings constitute the provisional (迹), while the Benevolent King of the Perfect Teaching constitutes the fundamental (本).

If one distinguishes between the fundamental (ben) and the derivative (ji), then the ten practices of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) can serve as the foundation for the Distinct Teaching (biejiao); the Buddha-ground of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao) is the derivative aspect of the Distinct Teaching; and the Two Vehicles of the Tripitaka Teaching (sanzang) are, in turn, the foundation within the Shared Teaching. Thus, each successive teaching possesses its own internal distinction between the fundamental and the derivative, and so forth.

As for "contemplating the mind," it means contemplating phenomena of arising and ceasing; seeing that form exists and analyzing it until it reaches emptiness, the mind attains mastery over form—this is the contemplation of the mind of arising and ceasing, the Benevolent King.
To contemplate that form is itself emptiness and that emptiness and form are sovereignly interpenetrating—this is the Benevolent King who contemplates the mind of non-arising.
To contemplate that emptiness is itself form and thereby enter the Middle Way through successive stages—this is the Benevolent King who contemplates the immeasurable mind.

If one contemplates that form is empty and emptiness is form—such that they are two yet not two, and non-dual despite being dual—and thus both illuminates them simultaneously and causes them both to vanish, this is the true mark of the single mind and the three contemplations, and the three contemplations within the single mind. Like those celestial eyes, which attain mastery without being either vertical or horizontal, this is the contemplation of the mind according to the Perfect Teaching, the Benevolent Kings Sūtra.

Our current Holy Lord’s transformation through the Way is boundless; he nurtures all living beings with benevolence and grace that permeates everywhere. He constantly uses the three contemplations to bring peace and security to both body and mind. His traces are already difficult to fathom, let alone his fundamental essence, which is truly hard to investigate.
“Prajñā” is translated here as “wisdom,” as explained in the forty-second fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*; both Kaishan and Master Zang adopted this interpretation.
In the seventieth treatise, there is another interpretation which says:
"The *prajñāpāramitā* is incalculable.
Because *prajñā* is extremely profound and exceedingly weighty, while wisdom (*jñāna*) is light and thin, it is therefore unable to weigh it."
Master Zhuangyan Min used this passage to argue that while the name *prajñā* encompasses manifold meanings, "wisdom" (*zhìhuì*) is merely one gateway and thus not a correct translation.
Examining the arguments of these two masters, each has formed a point of contention; I shall now provide a comprehensive resolution.
Now, Prajñā is of two kinds: first, the real;
second, the provisional.
The provisional may be translated, but the real cannot.
In reality, this refers to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), while the provisional refers to the three preceding teachings.
Furthermore, the provisional cannot be inverted; that is, the substantial form (*rūpa*) of the Tripitaka Teaching cannot be made such that "form is itself emptiness.

Reality, however, can be inverted; this refers to the three types of wisdom: the *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) of the Shared Teaching (*Tongjiao*), the *mārgajñatā* (knowledge of the paths) of the Distinct Teaching (*Biejiao*), and the *sarvākārajñatā* (knowledge of all modes) of the Perfect Teaching.
How can one rigidly adhere to a single perspective to confine the Great Way?
While the flames of fire cannot be grasped, it must truly exist somewhere.
Nevertheless, regarding *jñāna* (knowledge) and *prajñā* (wisdom), their interpretations differ across the sūtras and śāstras.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* explains this in combination, stating: "True wisdom is called knowledge (*jñāna*)," meaning that wisdom is itself knowledge.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* explains them separately: "Knowing the mental activities of all sentient beings, one preaches the Dharma according to their needs, giving rise to the activity of knowledge (*jñānakarman*), neither grasping nor rejecting, and entering the gate of the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇamukha*)."
Regarding the phrase "arising from the activity of wisdom," the commentary explains:
knowledge (*jñāna*) is existence and wisdom (*prajñā*) is emptiness. Because there is knowledge, one does not abide in emptiness; because there is wisdom, one does not abide in existence.
Now, this Prajñāpāramitā is fully translated in eight sections.
Some say that one section,
the *Devarāja*, is subsumed within the *Benevolent Kings* (*Renwang*) division.
This interpretation is untenable.
If it were as clarified in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, where it is stated that a human king is also a celestial king, then it would be acceptable.
Question:
Question: Since "human" (ren) and "benevolence" (ren) differ in their characters, how can they be taken as the same?
Answer:
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Because one possesses benevolent kindness, one is called a human."
The *Laozi* says, "The sage is not benevolent; he treats the common people as straw dogs.
Thus we know that when a king practices benevolence, he does not seek gratitude or recompense.
If one turns their back on the Master of the Way, then though a person may exist, they are not benevolent; if one follows the Master of the Way, then both the person and their benevolence exist.
Question:
What are benevolence and righteousness?
Answer:
When explaining meaning through the analysis of characters, the principle is easily clarified.
The upper character represents the virtue of Heaven, the lower character represents the virtue of Earth, and the character "ren" (人) signifies human virtue.
The Holy Sovereign’s Way equals that of the Creator, and his Virtue harmonizes with the Three Powers; thus he is called the Benevolent King (*Rājarāja*).
Question:
An ancient said that the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* is not a direct translation.
What do you say to this?
Answer:
Those of meager learning and small wisdom are deeply pitiable.
How can one fail to consult a catalog and yet immediately claim that a work is not a direct translation?
Haiyong did not believe that mountain wood could resemble fish, yet Xia Ge also claimed that in the primordial beginning there was nothing at all; alas, the blind man who ridicules the crystal bead!
Furthermore, according to the subsequent scriptures, there are two versions:

first, the extensive version, as stated in the "Chapter on Scattering Flowers": "At that time, the sixteen great kings, having heard the hundred trillion verses of the Prajñāpāramitā spoken by the Buddha, scattered flowers as an offering";
second, the abbreviated version, which is the text of the present scripture.
There are three different versions produced by various translators over time:

the first was translated during the Yongjia era of the Jin dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa (translated into Chinese as Fahu) of the Yuezhi; it consists of two fascicles and is titled *Renwang Prajñā*.

Second, in the third year of the Hongshi era of the spurious Qin dynasty, Kumārajīva translated two fascicles at the separate pavilion in the Xiaoyao Garden in Chang’an, titled *The Buddha-Spoken Prajñāpāramitā for Protecting the State by Benevolent Kings*.

Third, during the Liang dynasty, Paramārtha, at the request of Emperor Daoming, translated one fascicle titled the *Benevolent Kings Prajñā Sūtra* (*Renwang Banruo Jing*) at Shifensi in Yuzhang; its commentary consists of six fascicles.
Although there are three versions, the Qin edition is the most complete; this is stated according to Fei Changfang’s *Catalogue of Works Included in the Canon*.
As for "pāramitā," it is translated here as "the perfection of an undertaking," and is also called "reaching the other shore."

To take birth and death as "this," nirvana as "that," the afflictions as the "middle current," and the six perfections as the "boat or raft" is the explanation based on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

To take substantial existence as "this," the cessation of substantial existence as "that," the views and thoughts as the "middle current," and the Eightfold Noble Path as the "boat" is the explanation based on the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*).
In the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), form is taken as "this" and emptiness as "that"; the afflictions of view and thought are the middle current, and the six perfections are the boat.

In the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), form and emptiness are taken as "this," and emptiness being identical to form is taken as "that"; ignorance is the middle current, and immeasurable practices are the boat.

In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), that which is "this" is the non-duality of form and emptiness, yet their duality; that which is "that" is their non-duality despite their duality. Ignorance is the middle current; the single practice as infinite practices and infinite practices as a single practice constitute the boat.
To deliver beings according to the various preceding teachings is called "reaching the other shore.
This is an explanation based on the teachings (*jiao*).

Regarding the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*): whether one contemplates that form is itself empty or that form is extinguished into emptiness, although there may be differences in skill or clumsiness, both equally sever the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*), yet they are distinguished as "this" and "that."
The Contemplation of the Provisional (jiaguān) discusses the mutual relationship between self and other based on the attainment of the theory of the three provisionalities.
The Contemplation of the Middle (zhongguān) discusses the mutual relationship between self and other prior to the ten stages of faith and subsequent to the ten abodes.
This is the interpretation from the perspective of contemplating the mind.
The term *sūtra* (經) may be translated or left untranslated, each possessing five meanings, as explained at length in the *Fahua Xuan* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), and so forth.
In terms of the teachings (*jiao*), all six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) constitute a *sūtra*.
As the *Sūtra* states: "Or one may perform the Buddha-work through light," which means that the sense object of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*) constitutes a *sūtra*.
"To perform Buddha-work through sound" means that sound itself constitutes the sutra.
"To perform Buddha-work through the fragrance of food" means that the fragrance itself constitutes the sutra of the sensory object (gandha-viṣaya).
When food enters the throat, it is the passage of the sensory object of flavor;
when the lips move and the tongue stirs, it is the passage of the sensory object of touch;
when there is silence and no sound, and the various Bodhisattvas enter samādhi, it is the passage of the sensory object of mental phenomena (dharma).
Each individual sense organ and its object has its own interpretation according to the teaching (kyō), the fundamental and the manifested (honjaku), and the contemplation of the mind (kanjin).
Furthermore, taking the written words as the warp and mental practice as the woof, they form the fabric for attaining perfect enlightenment; thus, worldly scriptures are taken as a metaphor.
“Preface” (*xu*) means “origin” (*you*) or “sequence” (*ci*).
“Chapter” (*pin*) is called *varga* in Sanskrit, which here is translated as “chapter,” meaning a category.
When items of similar meaning and type follow one another, they constitute a single chapter.
The term "first" (di) is intended to prevent confusion;
"one" (yi) signifies that its meaning lies at the beginning.
The explanation of the names is complete.
Second, regarding the discernment of the essence: some say that the essence consists of the words and their meaning;
this is a general explanation.
Others say that the essence is the signless (animitta); since the signless exists in all four teachings, and as the signless is eternally pervasive, this too is a general explanation.
Some say that its essence consists of the five patiences (*kṣānti*) and the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

As the sutra below states: "The five patiences are the dharma of the bodhisattvas. Having enumerated the five patiences in full, it concludes by saying: "This is called the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā by all Buddhas and bodhisattvas. Therefore, we know that one realizes the five patiences through the cultivation of prajñā.
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not fail to become sages through the five patiences; therefore, the five patiences and ten stages constitute their essence (*tattva*).
Now, this is not so. First, let us explain the character "essence" (*ti*).
The "substance" (ti) is the Dharma; each person loves their own kin and each regards their own child as their own, while rulers and ministers exercise restraint.
If there were no substance, it would not be the Dharma.

The supramundane dharmas are likewise so: whether they be good or evil, ordinary beings or sages, bodhisattvas or Buddhas, none transcend the dharma-nature; they take the true mark (lakṣaṇa) as their very essence.
The *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra* states: "The cause of the Mahāyāna is the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena; the fruit of the Mahāyāna is likewise the true reality of all phenomena.

True reality is precisely the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). By relying on this dharma-nature as the cause, one attains the fruit of dharma-nature; therefore, it is known that this sutra takes true reality as its essence.
If discussed separately, there are two kinds of Prajñā:
first, that taught in common with followers of the Two Vehicles; second, that which is not shared [with them].
According to this principle, the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) likewise has two kinds:
There are two types: common and uncommon.
The common refers to seeing only emptiness and not seeing non-emptiness; it does not sever ignorance but only eliminates views and afflictions. This is the partial aspect of true reality.

The "unshared" refers to the Middle Way and the true mark (*dharmatā*). In the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavahāra*), it is cultivated sequentially prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and realized for the first time at the first stage (*bhūmi*).
In the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*), from the first dwelling (*vihāra*) up to the fruit of Buddhahood, it is practiced within a single mind and is termed "perfect realization" throughout.

If one discusses the provisional and the real, that which is common is the provisional aspect for the sake of transforming others, while that which is uncommon is the real aspect of one's own practice, and so forth.
In terms of the teachings, *prajñā* is universal, whereas it exists only in the Abhidharma-piṭaka [of the Tripiṭaka] and not elsewhere.
There are three vehicles that share the common practice of the ten stages (*bhūmi*): there is the separate entry into the common, and there is the perfect entry into the common.
The "common" is primary while the "separate" is secondary; thus, the Separate and Common [vehicles] are provisional (*upāya*), whereas the Perfect Teaching is the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
Although this sutra contains all three teachings, its true essence is the perfect and real mark (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*).
Third is the clarification of the school (*mūla*).
"School" means the essential core; specifically, it takes the Buddha’s own practice of cause and effect as its school.

There are those who take the correct contemplation of non-arising as their primary tenet, and who provisionally designate it as the "Middle Way" because it is free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "Prajñā is without cognition and without vision; it does not act and does not receive; it neither arises nor ceases."
This is the intent of the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna), which attains only the provisional while losing the real.

Now, taking the Buddha’s own practice of cause and effect as the essential core, we cause all who hear this to rejoice and increase their cultivation, so that every single form and scent is none other than Prajñā.

The true wisdom of *prajñā* is free from both existence and non-existence; yet, though it is free from existence and non-existence, existence and non-existence remain manifest within it. Although they remain manifest, they are themselves without marks (*animitta*). Therefore, it takes this markless causality as its fundamental tenet.
Question:
What is the difference between the "tenet" (zong) and the "essence" (ti)?
Answer:
The fundamental principle (*zong*) is like a fur cloak and its collar; the substance (*ti*) is like the hair and the eyes.
When the collar is shaken, the hair rises; when the eyes are moved, they open. Such is the relationship between the fundamental principle and the substance.
It is also like hairpins and bracelets: the gold and silver are the substance, while the artisan who fashions them is the fundamental principle.
Now, the principle of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the essence (*tattva*), while cultivating the causes and attaining the fruit constitutes the central tenet (*śāstra-prayojana*), and so forth.
Fourth, the analysis of function (*vṛtti*).
"Function" refers to efficacious power (*prabhāva*).
Some say that this sutra takes the two types of protection—internal and external—as its function.

Regarding internal protection, the subsequent text states: "For the sake of all bodhisattvas, it explains the causal conditions for protecting the fruit of Buddhahood and the causal conditions for protecting the practices of the ten stages."

Regarding "external protection," the subsequent text states: "I shall now explain for you the causes and conditions for protecting the state, so that the land may attain peace, the seven calamities do not arise, disasters do not occur, and the myriad people enjoy peace and happiness."
This is called "external protection.
Here, one obtains only one mundane and one true [protection], and even that true one is not fixed.
In the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect [teachings], all possess ten stages as protection.
Why is this? Because the ten stages (daśabhūmi) cannot serve as a complete basis.

Now, the two types of wisdom of all Buddhas function as the power and utility; for all Tathāgatas employ ultimate wisdom (jñāna) to illuminate themselves and expedient wisdom (upāya-jñāna) to illuminate others.

However, this sutra contains three types of provisional and ultimate [teachings]: although the Shared and Distinct [vehicles] possess ultimate wisdom, they are also termed provisional; and although the Perfect Teaching possesses the provisional, it is collectively designated as ultimate.

In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), these are the two wisdoms of the Buddha’s own practice: illuminating principle is itself discerning capacities, and discerning capacities is itself illuminating principle.

This is like when Śākyamuni [Sarbasi-da] drew King Anala’s bow to fullness, which is called "power"; piercing seven iron drums, penetrating Mount Cakravāḍa, and reaching through the earth to the waters is called "function."
The power and function of the common and specific [wisdoms] are weak, like the bow and arrow of an ordinary person. Why is this?

Because the common [wisdom] receives the two wisdoms for transforming others; it either illuminates the principle equally but not universally, or knows it only through successive stages. This is not equal to the Perfect Teaching’s perfect illumination and perfect realization; therefore, the two wisdoms within the Perfect [Teaching] are taken as its function.
That is to say, provisional wisdom protects the lands of the Shared Residence, the Land with Remainder, and the Land of True Reward, ensuring that the seven calamities do not arise;
whereas true wisdom protects the causes and effects of the forty-two minds of the Perfect Teaching.
The Sūtra states, "Protecting the causal conditions for the practice of the ten stages. This refers generally to the ten stages practiced according to the three teachings, and so forth.
Fifth, the clarification of the characteristics of the teachings.

To propagate the True Dharma, one must recognize the partiality and completeness of the teachings, as explained in detail in the *Fahua Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra); here, I shall briefly clarify it.
"Teaching" refers to the words spoken by the Sage for those below him.
"Characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refer to the differentiation of similarities and differences.

This sūtra belongs to the Prajñāpāramitā division; its teaching penetrates the Mahāyāna gate. It is a sūtra of the "matured butter" flavor, which explains the causes and conditions for protecting the fruit of Buddhahood and protecting the practices of the ten stages (bhūmi).
Furthermore, because the King asked Mahāyāna how it illuminates [reality], we know that this is not the illumination of the Tripiṭaka teaching.

Although there are eight verses discussing matters such as impermanence and arising-and-ceasing, these merely cite the past hundred Dharma masters who used the Hīnayāna to explain that the world is not solid, thereby exhorting Puming to renounce his kingdom; thus, they belong to the auxiliary path (upāya-mārga) and are not the primary exposition of the present sutra.
Next, we enter the textual exegesis.
Generally speaking, expository traditions in China differ: some divide the text into sections, while others do not.

For instance, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*’s commentary on the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* does not divide it into topical sections, whereas Vasubandhu’s *Nirvāṇa-śāstra* does indeed divide its text.
Dao’an separately established the Prologue, the Main Text, and the Circulation; Liu Qiu merely provided explanations following the text.
This is because human sentiments differ—like the orchid and the chrysanthemum—in their preferences; the intent lies in attaining the profound mystery rather than in engaging with worldly affairs.
Now, following the division of the text as an illustration:
when a sage expounds the Dharma, there must necessarily be a gradual progression; therefore, the Introduction (Nidāna) is explained first.
The Introduction reveals the main teaching and manifests its benefits for those present, which is called the Main Exposition (Saddharma-paryāya).
The section in which sentient beings of the final age equally receive the benefits of the Dharma is called the *pariṇāmanā* (circulation) section.

This sutra consists of eight chapters: the "Introductory Chapter" (*nidāna*) constitutes the introduction; the six chapters beginning with "Contemplating Emptiness" constitute the main exposition; and the "Chapter on Entrustment" (*parīndanā*) constitutes the circulation section.

If one looks at the scriptural text, the portion from the Buddha’s address to Candraprabha at the end of the "Chapter on Receiving and Upholding" onwards constitutes the *Pravartanā-vibhāga* (the section on dissemination), and so forth.
Now, the first two parts are the *Nidāna* (Introduction):

first, the *Śraddhā-nidāna* (Introduction of Faith); second, the *Utpatti-nidāna* (Introductory Narrative). These are also called the General Introduction and the Specific Introduction; alternatively, they are called the Tathāgata Introduction and the Ānanda Introduction; or else, the Introduction Prior to the Sūtra and the Introduction Subsequent to the Sūtra.

The six matters that authenticate the scripture are called the *Saddharmaprastāvanā* (序分, Prologue of Faith); that which initiates the main teaching is called the *Prastāvanā* (發起序, Prologue of Initiation);

that which is common to all scriptures is called the *Sāmānyaprastāvanā* (通序, General Prologue), while that which is unique to this scripture is called the *Vaiśeṣikaprastāvanā* (別序, Specific Prologue);

that which was spoken from the golden mouth is called the *Tathāgataprastāvanā* (如來序, Prologue of the Tathāgata), and that which is authenticated by Ānanda is called the *Ānandaprastāvanā* (阿難序, Prologue of Ānanda).
Because it existed during the time of the Buddha, it is called the "Preface to the Sūtra"; because it was added by the compilers, it is called the "Postscript to the Sūtra.
For now, we shall rely on the former, beginning from the words "Thus" (evam).
From "They all sat down" onwards is called the *Saddharmaprasthāna* (Sequence of Certainty and Faith).
From "At that time, [the Buddha with] the Ten Epithets" onwards is the *Nidāna* (Introductory Sequence).

Regarding the *Saddharmaprasthāna*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha was lying with his head to the north beneath the twin *sāla* trees in the kingdom of Kuśinagara, on the verge of entering *parinirvāṇa*."
At that time, Ānanda’s personal affection had not yet been eliminated, and his mind was submerged in an ocean of sorrow. Aniruddha said to Ānanda:
"You are a person who guards the treasury of the Dharma; you ought not, like an ordinary person, to sink yourself into an ocean of sorrow."
The Buddha is about to entrust the Dharma to you; yet now you are distressed and have lost sight of your duty.
You should ask the Buddha:
"After his parinirvāṇa, how shall we practice the Path?"
Who shall serve as preceptor?
How shall we dwell together with Chanda, who speaks such harsh words?
What words should be placed at the beginning of the Buddha’s discourses?
Having heard this, Ānanda’s dazed mind cleared slightly, and he questioned the Buddha in detail about the matter while lying on the bed behind him.
The Buddha replied:
“Abide by means of the four foundations of mindfulness.”
The *Vimokṣa-sūtra* and the precepts are the Great Master.
The bhikṣu Canda should discipline him according to the Brahma-faring Dharma.
If his mind requires reform, teaching him the *Kātyāyana-sūtra* will enable him to attain the Way.

This is the Dharma-treasure accumulated by me over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; first, one should establish the formula: "Thus have I heard at one time the Buddha was in such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a country, in such-and-such a place, in a grove of trees."
"In my Dharma-gate, this is what should be said at the outset. Why?
Because the sutras of the Buddhas of the three periods of time all contain these words, and so forth.
Furthermore, Mahākāśyapa and the others asked Ānanda:
"Where did the Buddha first preach the Dharma?
What kind of Dharma did he preach?
Ānanda replied:
"Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at the Deer Park of the Sages in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, where he taught the Noble Truth of Suffering to the five bhikṣus.
At that time, all those in the great assembly who heard it believed it.
This is as explained in detail in the second fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and so forth.
For this reason, there is the "Certification and Preface" (*samyak-saṃdhāna-nidāna*), and so forth.
The text consists of six parts:
First, "Thus" (evam) indicates the essence of the Dharma that was heard.
Second, "I heard" (śrutam mayā) clarifies Ānanda as the one who maintains it.
Third, "at one time" (ekasmin samaye) clarifies the harmonious convergence of hearing and maintaining, wherein the path of resonance and response is met.
4. "The Buddha" clarifies the master who proclaims the teaching.
5. From "Residing in the city of Rājagṛha" downward, it clarifies the place where the teaching is proclaimed.
6. From "Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus" downward, it clarifies the assembly that hears the teaching together.

Regarding the explanation of these six phrases: the sutras of the Buddhas of the three periods all conclude with "Thus [have I heard]"; the paths of all Buddhas are identical, and they do not contend with the world—this is the *loka-samvṛti-satya* (worldly standpoint).
The *Mahā-śāstra* states: "To cite the time and place so as to inspire faith in people is the *puruṣa-siddhānta*.
To refute the two characters 'ā' and 'u' of the non-Buddhists is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*."
Sengzhao said:
"Suchness (evam) is a term for faith and compliance.
Through faith, the principles one has heard are harmonized; through compliance, the way between teacher and disciple is perfected."
"Understanding this principle is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint).
These four are all explained through the lens of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and so forth.

Regarding the classification by teaching (*yōkyō*): the Buddha clarifies that conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) possesses words and letters, while ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is devoid of words and letters. Ānanda transmitted the Buddha’s conventional words without alteration, which is termed "Suchness" (*tathatā*). By means of these conventional words, one realizes the ultimate; because there is nothing that is not [the ultimate], it is called "is" (*sho*)."
"In the beginning was thus" refers to the sūtras of the Tripitaka Teaching.

The Buddha clearly elucidated that form is emptiness and emptiness is form; that form and emptiness, being empty and yet possessing form, are non-dual and without distinction; and that the non-differentiation of emptiness and form constitutes "Suchness" (tathatā), while the realization of reality within phenomena constitutes "Thusness" (tathā). This refers to the sūtras of the Shared Teaching. "In the beginning was thus."

The Buddha taught that birth-and-death is existence and nirvana is non-existence; one enters the non-existence of nirvana from the existence of birth-and-death, and emerges from the non-existence of nirvana to enter the Middle Way. Ānanda’s transmission of this was no different from the Buddha’s own. Such is the beginning of this distinct teaching scripture.

The Buddha taught that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa and the Middle Way; that which pervades all places and is nothing other than the Buddha-dharma is called the "True Aspect" (yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa). Ānanda’s transmission of this is no different from the Buddha’s own, and thus it is "as-it-is" (tathatā); being suchness, immovable, it is termed "thus" (iti). This is the opening formula of the Perfect Teaching (pūrṇa-yāna) sūtras: "Thus have I heard."
This sutra fully possesses the meaning of the three teachings and the three truths; thus, Ānanda’s transmission of it is without error or deviation.
This concludes the exposition on the essence of the Dharma as heard.

Regarding the explanation of "I have heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*): the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states, "Because the faculty of the ear is unimpaired, the sound is within the range of hearing, and the mind is directed toward listening—through the convergence of these various conditions, one says 'I have heard.'"
"I summarize the particulars within the general and employ the general to encompass the particulars"—this is the worldly interpretation.
Ānanda ascends the seat and declares "I have heard," while the great assembly weeps and utters verses from mid-air; this refers to human beings.
When Ānanda ascended the seat, the assembly doubted whether Śākyamuni was arising again, or whether Ānanda had attained Buddhahood, or whether a Buddha from another direction had arrived;
once he uttered "Thus have I heard," these three doubts were immediately dispelled—this is the explanation as an antidote.

Ānanda followed worldly convention by saying, "Thus have I heard. Yet, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the "I" is no-self and "hearing" is no-hearing; it is hearing without hearing and being a self without a self. This is the explanation according to the ultimate truth.

Regarding the provisional teaching, the *Śāstra* states: "Ordinary beings have three types—namely, those of view, pride, and name; those in training have two types; and those beyond training have one type."

"Ānanda is a seeker (śaikṣa) who is free from the false self and is able to subdue the pride of 'I'; he uses the term 'I' merely in accordance with worldly conventions—this is the intent of the Tripiṭaka.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states: 'To employ the four phrases of "I" is to fall into false views.'"
"In the Buddha’s True Dharma, there is no self; who then hears it?
This is the intent of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The learned Ānanda can naturally understand and realize both 'self' and 'non-self.'"
"To know self and non-self as two yet not-two, dualistically discriminating between self and non-self—this is the meaning of the Separate Teaching (biejiao).

If Ānanda knows self and non-self as not-two yet two, and two yet not-two, thereby serving as an attendant to transmit the Buddha’s wisdom—this is the interpretation of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao)."
In the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, there are three Ānandas:
first, Ānanda, which means "Joyful," who upholds the Śrāvaka-piṭaka;
second, Ānandabhadra, which means "Virtuous Joyful," who upholds the Kṣudraka-piṭaka.
Third is Ānanda Sāgara, which in this language means "Ocean of Joy"; he upholds the Buddha-piṭaka.
Among the Āgamas, there is the Ānanda of the Mahānidāna who upholds the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
This refers clearly to a single person who possesses four virtues and transmits four teachings.
As for the contemplation of the mind, it consists of the contemplation of emptiness, the contemplation of the provisional, and the correct contemplation of the Middle Way.
That which is emptiness is precisely non-self;
that which is the conventional is precisely non-self as self;
that which is the middle way is the true self.

Regarding "having heard": Ānanda, you were born on the night the Buddha attained the Way and have attended upon him for over twenty years; before attending upon the Buddha, you surely had not heard it.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Ānanda heard [the teachings] through successive transmission; he did not hear them all.
In the *Baoen jing*, Ānanda requested four vows, among which was his vow that the Buddha would re-explain any teachings he had not yet heard.

The *Garbha-sūtra* states: "The Buddha extended a golden arm from his golden coffin and once again manifested for Ānanda the signs of entering and emerging from the womb; because of this, all the sūtras came to be known as 'heard' (*śruta*)."

The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "When Ānanda received his prediction, he immediately recollected the Buddha-dharma of the past, causing it to appear as if before his eyes; therefore, everyone heard and proclaimed it."
This is the explanation by way of causes and conditions.

If Ānanda rejoices, his face is like the pure full moon and his eyes are like blue lotuses; he personally receives the Buddha’s instructions as one might look up while pouring water from a full vessel into another jar, without missing a single word.
This is upholding the Dharma that has been heard while hearing it.

Abiding joyfully in the stage of training (śaikṣabhūmi), one attains emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; with the six sense faculties unimpaired, one upholds the Dharma that has not been heard while hearing it.
The Elder Ānanda has received and retained a vast treasury of teachings, like clouds holding rain; he maintains this "hearing of the unheard" Dharma.
The Elder Ānanda is an ocean of learning; naturally, he is able to comprehend such things as the permanent and the impermanent.
If one knows that the Tathāgata never preaches the Dharma, this is called "much hearing.
The waters of the great ocean of the Buddha-Dharma flow into Ānanda’s mind; this is the upholding of the Dharma that is neither heard nor not heard.
"This sutra possesses the three teachings; that is to say, Ānanda alone transmitted and upheld them through the three virtues," and so forth.
Regarding the explanation of "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*), Sengzhao said:
"The day the Dharma King inaugurated his mandate, the occasion when the great assembly gathered in auspicious conclave."
This is the time for explaining this world.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Kāla refers to actual time; it indicates the time for teaching the inner disciples, the time for eating, and the time for putting on robes—these are the times for speaking to people."
"Samaya is a conventional designation for time, intended to exclude those with the false views of non-Buddhists.
This is an explanation of "time" by way of its therapeutic function (*pratipakṣa*).
Within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is neither time nor non-time.
A detailed explanation of the meaning of "time" is fully set forth in the first fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and so forth.

According to the classification of teachings (*yàojiào*), the period from those who have realized the truths (*dijian*) up to those below the stage of no-more-learning (*wuxué*) is called the "lower one-time";
if three persons enter the primary truth (*diyiyi*) together, it is called the "middle one-time."
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward is called the "upper one-time";
from the first abode (*vihāra*) upward is called the "uppermost one-time.

The initial teaching in this sutra refers to the "universal one-time," yet when categorized according to the distinct and perfect [teachings] and their points of entry, it possesses all three times, and so forth.
The teacher of the Śākya school is the Buddha. "Buddha" means "Awakened";

one awakens from the two maladies of afflictions—the body and the mind—and only when cause and effect are perfected can one break the bonds. At the beginning of a kalpa there is no illness, while at the end of a kalpa there is much illness; during times of true longevity there is happiness, while during times of short life there is suffering. In the eastern continent (Pūrvavideha) people are wealthy but short-lived; in the western continent (Aparagoyānī) there are many cattle and sheep; in the northern continent (Uttarakuru) there is neither self nor person. In such places, the Buddha cannot manifest.

When the human lifespan was eighty thousand years, people in Jambudvīpa practiced the causes before seeing the fruits; this remained so even until the time when the lifespan was one hundred years. Therefore, the Buddha appeared in that land; this is the explanation of the world of Śākya.
If the sun were not to rise, the flowers in the pond—those yet to bloom and those already grown—would all remain unmanifest; once the sun rises, they all come to life.
If the Buddha were not to appear in the world, devas and humans would diminish, while the evil realms would increase.
If a Buddha appears in the world, there will be kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, the four heavenly kings, and so on up to the Peak of Existence; these are the human Śākyas.

Those with the faculties and dispositions of the three vehicles can evoke the appearance of a Buddha in the world, whereas others cannot; if one cuts off the seeds of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one will forever cross over the stream of birth and death—this is the explanation by way of antidote (*pratipakṣa*).

The Buddha is neither moved nor emerges from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), yet he enables sentient beings to perceive movement and emergence; yet for the Tathāgata, there is truly no movement or emergence—this is the teaching of the ultimate truth (paramārtha).

The Buddha is called the Awakened One because he has awakened to the suffering and its origin in the world, and awakened to the path and its cessation that transcend the world. His body is sixteen feet tall, and his lifespan is eighty years.

Appearing in the form of a bhikṣu, he attained Buddhahood beneath the tree through thirty-four moments of mind; as for the World-Honored One of the Tripiṭaka, he is one who has awakened himself and awakened others.

Carrying the sixteen-foot image, he manifests the *viśeṣa-kāya* (body of excellence); upon the tree, through a single thought of resonance, he severs all remaining habitual tendencies, thereby attaining the Buddha’s self-awakening and awakening of others.
To manifest the sublime body of the Honored One, sitting upon a lotus pedestal and receiving the prediction of Buddhahood, is the distinct Buddha’s self-awakening and awakening of others.
To conceal the previous three marks and manifest only the inconceivable mark like space is the Perfect Teaching Buddha’s self-awakening and awakening of others.

Therefore, the *Sūtra on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Semblance Dharma* states: "One may see a body sixteen feet tall; or see a small body or a large body; or see [the Buddha] seated upon a lotus pedestal, expounding the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground for hundreds of thousands of Śākyamunis; or see the body filling all of space, pervading the entire Dharma-realm without any discrimination."
This refers to the meaning of the four Buddhas.
Regarding the interpretation in terms of the provisional (迹) and the fundamental (本): the three Buddhas are the provisional, and the one Buddha is the fundamental, and so forth.

Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: to contemplate phenomena produced by causes and conditions and analyze them until they reach non-existence—this is the "clumsy awakening" of the Tripitaka [teaching].
To contemplate causes and conditions as empty is the skillful awakening of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), wherein all realize emptiness.
If one first contemplates emptiness, then the provisional (provisional existence), and finally the Middle Way, this is the provisional awakening of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao).
If one contemplates all phenomena as being simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle Way, this is Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
The dwelling place is explained in three parts:
first, the explanation of "dwelling"; second, the explanation of the "royal city"; and third, the explanation of the "mountain."
The Buddha possesses the three bodies (trikāya), and his abodes are eightfold.
The four abodes of the response body (nirmāṇakāya) are:
first, the abode of life-span, which refers to the fivefold dharma-body (pañcadharmakāya) and so forth.
Second is abiding by way of support, which refers to royal cities, Mount Grdhrakūṭa, and so forth.
Third is abiding by way of objective sphere, which refers to the objective sphere of the trichiliocosm.
Fourth is abiding by way of deportment, which refers to walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.
The Sambhogakāya has three abodes:
first, the celestial abode, which dwells in the six heavens of the desire realm;
second, the Brahma abode, which dwells in the heavens of the four dhyānas.
Third is the Noble Abode (*āryavihāra*), which dwells in emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
The Dharma-body has a single abode, dwelling in the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), and so forth. Regarding the classification by teaching (*yōkyō*):

the Buddha of the Tripitaka [Teaching] develops true knowledge through the gate of analytical negation and dwells in the two nirvāṇas with and without remainder; the Buddha of the Shared Teaching develops the truth through the gate of essence and dwells in the two nirvāṇas; the Buddha of the Distinct Teaching dwells in the Secret Treasury through the gate of sequential progression; and the Buddha of the Perfect Teaching dwells in the Secret Treasury through the gate of non-sequential progression.
Second, the explanation of the city.
To preserve the original Sanskrit sounds, it should be called Rājagṛha-mahāgira.
Rājagṛha means "King’s Abode" (Wángshè) in this language.
Mahā means "great" in this language. Kara means "city.
The name of the country is Magadha, which means "one who does not harm people," as there is no law of chaotic killing there.
He is also called Magadha; this is translated as Tianluo (Devila). Tianluo was the father of Panzu (Suprabuddha).

Long ago, in times of yore, this man ruled over a thousand small kingdoms. Once, while the king was out hunting, he encountered a female lion with whom he had intercourse. Later, when her month was full, she came to the king’s palace and gave birth to a son there.
King Shenzhi was his father, yet he issued a proclamation stating:
"I had no son; Heaven has granted me this son.
He raised him until he grew up; because there were white spots on his feet, people of the time called him Banzu (Spotted Feet).

Later, when he succeeded to the throne, he took great pleasure in eating meat. Once, when his supply was suddenly exhausted, he had a recently deceased infant from west of the city taken to provide for the king’s meal.
The king found it most delicious and issued an edict that this practice should henceforth be made a regular rule.
From that day forward, the cook killed one person daily, and his poison spread throughout the world until the entire nation was filled with resentment.
A thousand minor kings raised armies to attack him, and he was exiled to the Five Mountains.
Supported by rākṣasas as his ministers, he became a king of ghosts; he had previously made a vow with a mountain deity to slay a thousand kings in order to fulfill his wish.
He immediately used his supernatural powers to capture various kings, until finally King Puming was seized. He intended to slaughter him as a sacrifice for the mountain deity.
At that time, King Samantaprabha wept with grief and lamentation, saying:
"I have always spoken the truth since birth, yet now my word has been violated. Pan-zu asked:
"What kind of faith do you seek?
Puming replied,
"I have vowed to practice great giving."
Pāṇḍuka said, "Release me so that I may practice giving; when the task is finished, come to me.

Pūrvaprabhāsa rejoiced and returned to his own country from afar. He established a great assembly for almsgiving, entrusted the governance to his crown prince, and with a peaceful mind and a joyful body, crawled on his hands and knees until his end.
Banzu asked,
"The gate of death is difficult to face.
Since you were able to leave it, why have you come back here again?"

At that time, King Samantaprabha extensively expounded upon the mind of loving-kindness and compassion to Pāda, censuring the act of killing and demonstrating that all things are entirely impermanent.
Having heard and believed this, Pāda attained the equality of emptiness and dwelt in the first stage (bhūmi).

The thousand kings assembled together; each took a drop of blood and three strands of hair to offer as a vow to the mountain deity. Thereupon, they built a city and established dwellings within the Five Central Mountains among the thousand kings, flourishing as a great nation where they took turns governing the state.
Because a thousand kings resided there, it was called Rājagṛha (King’s House).
Furthermore, although the houses of the common people within the city were built seven times and burned down seven times, only the King’s House alone was spared.
The Crown Prince issued a decree, saying:
"From this day forward, although the homes of all commoners shall be called Rājagṛha, they shall be exempt from the calamity of fire.
Consequently, throughout the land, by virtue of this command, they were spared from burning; thus, the homes of all commoners came to be known as Rājagṛha, and so forth.
Furthermore, it is also called "Royal Amnesty" (Rāja-kṣānti) because King Viśvabhū released a thousand kings, hence the name "Royal Amnesty.
Moreover, this city was built by the Four Heavenly Kings together; therefore, it is called "Rājagṛha" (the Abode of Kings).

Furthermore, the King of Magadha gave birth to a son who had one head, two faces, and four hands; considering him an ill omen, they tore apart his body and head, intending to cast them away into the wilds.
There was a rākṣasī named Ilā who reunited his body and nourished him with her milk.

When he grew up to adulthood, his strength surpassed that of all kingdoms. He captured eighty-four thousand kings and established a city within the Five Mountains to govern them; because many kings resided there, it was called Rājagṛha (the Abode of Kings), and so forth.
Furthermore, Magadha is named the Land Holding the Ambrosia (Amṛta).

It contains twelve great cities: first, the great city of Rājagṛha; second, the great city of Pūrṇabhadra; third, the great city of Āmrapālī; fourth, the great city of Vārāṇasī; fifth, the great city of Śrāvastī; sixth, the great city of Vārāṇasī; seventh, the great city of Vārāṇasī; eighth, the great city of Kapilavastu; ninth, the city of Campā; tenth, the city of Vatsa; eleventh, the city of Kauśāmbī; and twelfth, the city of Kuru.
Among these twelve cities, the latter six are places where he dwells for short periods, while the former six are places where he dwells for long periods.
Furthermore, among the first six cities, he dwells most frequently in Rājagṛha in order to repay the debt of gratitude to his Dharma-body;
he dwells less frequently in Śrāvastī in order to repay the debt of gratitude to his birth-body.
Regarding "Śrāvastī," there were six monasteries within the city of Rājagṛha:
first, the Bamboo Grove Monastery (Veṇuvana), situated on level ground and built by the elder Kalandaka, located thirty *li* northwest of the city;
second, the Lesser Hill of Solitary Power Monastery; [and so forth].
1. The Cave Mountain Hermitage of the Thirty-seven Leaves;
2. The Cave Mountain Hermitage of the Four Heavenly Kings;
3. The Cave Mountain Hermitage of the Snake Deity.
Sixth is the vihāra on Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain.
Gṛdhrakūṭa is translated here as "Spiritual Vulture Peak.
In the past, when Śākyamuni was a bodhisattva, he served as a vulture on this mountain to nourish and raise his parents; it was named from this circumstance, hence the name "Spiritual Vulture Peak."
Furthermore, to the south of Rājagṛha there was a Śītavana cemetery where vultures dwelt and frequently fed upon the dead.
When a person was about to die, the vultures would soar over their house and utter mournful cries; thus, people could know it in advance.
Because it was known that people died there, it is called Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak).

Furthermore, the mountain has five peaks: Elephant Head in the east, Horse Head in the south, Goat Head in the west, Lion Head in the north, and Vulture Head in the center; for this reason as well, it is named Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Mountain).
Question:
For what reason did the Buddha specifically go from the royal city to Vulture Peak to teach the Dharma?
Answer:

According to the *Dharmapada-sūtra-śāstra*, it says: "Just as Rājagṛha City excels other cities and Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain excels other mountains, because the Buddha dwells in these superior places, this Dharma-gate is revealed to be supreme."
Since this Prajñā is the most supreme dharma, it is specifically taught here at the Royal City and Vulture Peak Mountain.
The term "Middle" indicates that the Middle Way Prajñā is being expounded.
"Accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus," and so forth: this sixth section lists the assembly of those who heard the teaching together.
In all sūtras, the listing of assemblies does not exceed four types:

first, the "echoes and reflections," referring to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas whose great fruits are already perfected; they come as echoes and reflections in order to cause the True Dharma to abide long in the world.

Second, the assembly of those with whom a karmic connection has been established: although they hear the teaching while present, they do not yet obtain benefit; it merely serves as the causal condition for attaining the Way in the future.
Third, the assembly of initiators: Dharma-body Bodhisattvas mutually inspire one another to request the Tathāgata to preach, so that all may together benefit sentient beings.

Fourth, as for the assembly of those who are the proper recipients: having planted the causes in remote antiquity, they have brought forth the fruit in this present life; thus, at the very moment of hearing the Dharma, they are able to awaken and enter [the truth].
Regarding the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, each has four meanings which can be understood by applying this principle.
The text consists of two parts:
first, the listing of the assembly; second, the general conclusion.
The first part has three sections:
First, the assembly of this land; second, the assembly from other regions; third, the transformed assembly.
The first section is divided into three parts:
first, the assembly of śrāvakas; second, the assembly of bodhisattvas; third, the assembly of various classes of beings.

The two vehicles are listed first because they are attached to emptiness; ordinary beings are listed last because they are attached to existence; and bodhisattvas are listed in the middle because they constantly practice the Middle Way.

Furthermore, śrāvakas are first because both their minds and forms are superior; bodhisattvas are in the middle because their minds are superior while their forms are inferior; and ordinary beings are last because both their minds and forms are inferior.
The first section has two parts:
first, the śrāvakas; second, the pratyekabuddhas.
The first part has five sections:
This section consists of five parts: first, the title; second, the enumeration; third, the positions of the lines; fourth, the praise of virtues;
and fifth, the summary. Now, for the first part: "With" (yǔ) signifies "together with."
The *Śāstra* states: "At one time, in one place, with one precept, one mind, one view, one path, and one liberation.
As for "Great" (*mahā*), it may also be called "many" (*bahu*) or "superior" (*viśiṣṭa*).

They are called "Great" because they are all Arhats; they are said to be "many" because their number reaches eight hundred million billion; and they are called "victorious" because they surpass all other heterodox paths.
Regarding the term "Bhikṣu," there are five meanings:
first, he is a "mendicant" (bhikṣu), who maintains a pure livelihood by avoiding the four types of wrong sustenance.
Second, he destroys afflictions because views and craving have been extinguished.
Third, regarding his name and title: just as there are distinct names for different forms, such as those in Sanskrit and Chinese, so too does he have a specific designation.
Fourth, because he has received the full precepts (*upasampadā*), he is called a bhikṣu.
Fifth, "bhikṣu" is interpreted as "one who is capable" and "one who terrifies. Because he is capable of terrifying the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*), he is called a bhikṣu.
Four or more persons are termed a "saṃgha," and so forth.
“Eight hundred million billion” refers to the second enumeration of the number.
Regarding the phrase “those in training and those beyond training” (*śaikṣa-aśaikṣa*) that follows, this is the third [section], clarifying their stages of practice.
Since they are described as both those in training and those beyond training, why are they all referred to as *arhats*?

According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, there are two types of arhats: first, those who abide, and second, those who practice. It should be understood that those who practice are learners (*śaikṣa*), while those who abide are those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The virtuous who observe the five precepts all practice as Arhats," which refers precisely to those in training (śaikṣa).

Furthermore, within this context, a single passage first clarifies that moral conduct constitutes both those in training and those beyond training (aśaikṣa); because such a person trains in the conduct of one beyond training, it does not carry the meaning of a "candidate" (pratipannaka).

Among the eight types of persons, those of the four stages of approach and the three fruits are called "those in training" (*śaikṣa*) and "those beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*); the eighth, the Arhat, is exclusively "beyond training.
Regarding the phrase "all are Arhats," it overturns three meanings:
first, "non-arising. Having shed the husk of ignorance, they will no longer undergo rebirth within the field of future existences; therefore, they are said to be "non-arising."
Second, they are "slayers of thieves," so called because they have exhausted the ninety-eight latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) of affliction;
third, they are "worthy of offerings," for being fully endowed with wisdom and vows, they are capable of digesting the offerings of sentient beings.
This is the meaning according to the Tripiṭaka and Shared Teachings (Zàngtōng).
If explained according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuán), it is not only non-arising, but also the non-arising of non-arising; that which is untainted (anāsrava) is non-arising.
It is not only the slaying of thieves, but also the slaying of those who are not thieves; "those who are not thieves" refers to Nirvana.
"It is not only for the Arhats, but also for the sustenance of all sentient beings; this is 'provisioning' (sāmagrī), and so forth.
Regarding the section "conditioned merit" (*saṃskṛta-puṇya*) below, there are four praises of its virtues.
The text contains eight topical sections on the Dharma gates, which may also be used to praise three types of persons.

The first four sections praise those of the Shared Teaching; the next three sections on the "Three Provisions" praise those of the Distinct Teaching; and the final section on the "Three Emptinesses" praises those of the Perfect Teaching.

Furthermore, the first four sections praise the common [teachings], while from "the provisional nature of dharmas" (*dharmaprajñapti*) onwards, they collectively praise the distinct and the perfect [teachings].
The first section is divided into four parts;
here, at the outset, there is the praise of the merits of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The conditioned refers to the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), while the unconditioned pertains to the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
If discussed in terms of their objects, the Truth of the Path is conditioned, and the Truth of Cessation is unconditioned.
Giving things is called "merit" (*gu*), and attributing them to oneself is called "virtue" (*ṇa*); thus, they are termed "meritorious virtues" (*guṇa*).
Following "The Ten Knowledges of One Beyond Training," there next follows a praise of the distinctions among these knowledges.

Regarding the "ten knowledges": first is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*). This refers to the untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) regarding phenomena bound to the desire realm; untainted knowledge regarding the causes bound to the desire realm; untainted knowledge regarding the cessation of phenomena bound to the desire realm; untainted knowledge regarding the path for abandoning phenomena bound to the desire realm; and untainted knowledge within the category of the knowledge of phenomena itself.
Second is inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*); within the paths of the two higher realms, it is termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*) when untainted (*anāsrava*).

Regarding the middle [truths], four types of untainted knowledge are distinguished according to the Four Noble Truths, as clarified above in the section on dharma-knowledge; there is only the distinction between dharma-knowledge and inferential knowledge.

Third is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*); it knows the present minds and mental factors (*caitta*) bound to the two realms of desire and form, as well as a small portion of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors; this is termed the knowledge of others' minds.

Fourth is the knowledge of the world (*lokajñāna*), which is the wisdom regarding the outflow-tainted phenomena of all worlds; it is also called conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) because it is possessed equally by both ordinary persons and sages.
Fifth is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), which contemplates the five aggregates as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.

Sixth is the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*), which is untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) when contemplating the cause, the origin, the arising, and the condition of tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
Seventh is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), which is untainted wisdom when contemplating exhaustion, cessation, the sublime, and emergence.
The knowledge of the Eightfold Path is the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that arises at the time of contemplating the path as the correct track and vehicle.

The ninth is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), which consists of having seen suffering, having abandoned its origin, having realized its cessation, and having cultivated the path, and so forth.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "I have seen suffering, abandoned its origin, realized its cessation, and cultivated the path.
The ten knowledges of non-arising mean that having seen suffering, one does not see it again, and so forth.
In various sutras, it is sometimes said that there are eleven knowledges (*jñāna*).

The *Prajñāpāramitā* is the knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtajñāna*). It knows the general and specific characteristics of all phenomena; knowing them correctly and truly without any obstruction is what constitutes "as-it-is-ness" (*yathābhūta*).
These exist exclusively within the Buddha’s mind and are not shared by those of the Two Vehicles; therefore, they are simply called the "ten knowledges.

As for the "eight knowledges of those in training," this refers to the Anāgāmin who, while in the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), lacks the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*); thus, they possess only eight.

"Having the six knowledges of those in training" refers to the fact that within the path of seeing (darśanamārga), there are only the four truths and the six knowledges, such as the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
"The three faculties" refers to the subsequent praise of the virtues of the three faculties.

If one follows the sequence of practice, one should first distinguish the three faculties (*indriya*) and subsequently distinguish the ten knowledges (*jñāna*); here, however, the fruit is explained first and the cause is clarified later.

First is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*): when those who follow the path of faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or the path of Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) combine the nine untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is termed the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
The nine faculties refer to the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), as well as joy (*prīti*), pleasure (*sukha*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the mental faculty (*manas*).

Regarding the two faculties of knowledge (*ājñendriya*): for those who have attained through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) or through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), these same nine faculties are designated as the faculties of knowledge during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), as previously explained.

Regarding the "three knowledges" (*jñāna*), when one reaches the stage of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), these nine faculties (*indriya*) are renamed as the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*), and so forth.
As for the "sixteen mental activities," this next section praises the sixteen gates of contemplation (*ṣoḍaśākāra*).
Because it proceeds from what the mind performs, it is called "mental activity" (*cittābhisaṃskāra*); it does not mean that the mind itself is the activity.
According to the sequence of practice, it should be explained before the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*), as it is also the fruit that is taught first.
Furthermore, the sixteen aspects (ākāra) are simply the four truths separated out; "aspect" (ākāra) has the meaning of proceeding toward [an object].
By practicing these sixteen methods of contemplation, one is able to proceed toward the principle of the four realities; therefore, they are called "aspects."
The four aspects under "Suffering" (duḥkha) are:
first, impermanence; second, suffering; third, emptiness; fourth, non-self.
The four aspects under "Origination" (samudaya) are:
First, accumulation; second, cause; third, condition; fourth, arising.
Regarding cessation, there are four aspects:
first, exhaustion; second, cessation; third, excellence; fourth, escape.
The four aspects of the Path are: first, the path; second, the rightness; third, the track; and fourth, the vehicle.
Furthermore, there are sixteen aspects such as the acceptance of dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*); this is explained according to the general [classification].

If the forty stages prior to the bhūmis are counted as four, the ten bhūmis as ten, and equal-enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) and wondrous-enlightenment (vimala-bodhi) as sixteen, this is according to a distinct classification, and so forth.
Commentary on the Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the Protection of the State, Scroll One.
Commentary on the Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the Protection of the State, Scroll Two.
Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai; recorded by his disciple Guanding.
Below "The Contemplation of the Provisionality, Emptiness, and Reality of Dharmas," next follows the praise of the gate of the three types of contemplation on provisionality.
"Provisionality of dharmas" refers to the dharma of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). "Provisionality of persons" refers to the four [remaining] aggregates (*skandhas*).
Taking these two names, it is called the "provisionality of name" (*nāma-prajñapti*).
It has no self-substance in reality; it exists only by depending on others, and thus it is called provisional.

Furthermore, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is the "dharma," while sensation (*vedanā*) and the others are "names. Within all the world, there are only names and forms, yet here we speak of three distinct categories, and so forth.
Regarding the terms "false" and "real," there is first the false and second the real; these designations arise through mutual contrast.
The dharmas of the aggregates (skandhas) are false, yet ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) call them real; though one seeks to understand them through wisdom, they cannot be found.
To take the real as empty is called "empty-reality"; this is the general meaning.
If one explains the specific meanings, there are three contemplations within each of the three provisionalities (*prajñapti*).
The provisionality of phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti*) is precisely emptiness; this is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), wherein emptiness is itself the reality of the provisional.

That every form and every fragrance is none other than *prajñā* is the contemplation of the provisional (*jia-guan*); the single character "contemplation" (*guan*) itself is the contemplation of the middle (*zhong-guan*).

Because emptiness and the provisional constitute the path of skillful means (*upāya-mārga*), they are not designated as "contemplations"; only upon entering the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) do they alone receive the title of "contemplation."
The categories of sensation (*vedanā*) and name (*nāman*), and so forth, can be understood in this way.

To speak exhaustively, the three dharmas are themselves emptiness, themselves the provisional, and themselves the middle; they consist in the simultaneous illumination and simultaneous transcendence of both, and so on.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "All phenomena are not real; ordinary beings are false and illusory. Through recollection, thought, and discrimination, they falsely claim there is a person, like a dog at a well barking at its own reflection."
"In the water there was no dog, only its reflected image; yet he gave rise to an evil thought, threw himself into the well, and died. Sentient beings are likewise:

the harmony of the four great elements is called a "body," and through the principle of dependent origination, it produces movement and speech. Yet ordinary people falsely give rise to the notion of a "person" within this; these phenomena are merely provisional.
The arising of craving and aversion, the production of delusion and pleasure, and falling into the three evil realms—these are the conventional designations of sensation (*vedanā*).

Furthermore, all phenomena arise merely from the combination of names; there is no other name beyond this. For example, because the head, feet, belly, and spine combine, they are conventionally designated as a "body. Because hair, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, skin, and bones combine, they are conventionally designated as a "head. The collection of various hairs is conventionally designated as "hair," and the joining of these parts is conventionally designated as "hairs. The collection of various particles of dust is conventionally designated as "parts," and likewise, the collection of these parts is called "dust. This is the conventional designation of names (*nāma-prajñapti*).
Because these are provisional, all phenomena are empty.

Regarding the phrase "the three emptinesses" and so forth, this next section praises the virtues of samādhi; it receives the name of the "three emptinesses" due to the causes and conditions of the three kinds of provisional existence. This is an explanation of the sequence of cause and effect.
Because phenomena are provisional, they are empty; because sensation is provisional, it is signless; because designation is provisional, it is wishless.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "By means of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, one enters the gate to nirvāṇa."
There are three gates to nirvāṇa, namely emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). Regarding the gate of emptiness:

one contemplates that all phenomena (*dharma*) are devoid of self (*ātman*) and what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*); that all phenomena exist through the combination of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-samavāya*), and that there is no agent (*kartṛ*) and no experiencer (*bhoktṛ*). This is called the gate of emptiness.

Regarding the gate of signlessness (*animitta-mukha*): although one contemplates that the body is empty, signs (*nimitta*) still persist; because people are attached to these signs, they cultivate signlessness. As it is said, in the acts of looking up and down, bending and stretching, standing, walking, coming and going, observing, and speaking, there is no reality within them.

As for the statement that "the wind has its functions because it relies on consciousness," this refers to the characteristic of the cessation of consciousness, as it is non-existent from moment to moment.

This notion of a self in men and women arises from the mind lacking wisdom and thus falsely perceiving existence; [in reality,] the skeleton is linked together and covered by skin and flesh, moving like a wooden puppet through its mechanisms. This is the gate of signlessness (*animitta*).
Regarding the gate of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*): when even the signless (*animitta*) is absent, this is called non-action.

Among these three concentrations within the various dhyānas, if they are absent, they are not called samādhis; because of such retrogression and loss, one falls back into the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

As it is said: one who is able to uphold pure precepts is called a bhikṣu; one who is able to contemplate emptiness is called a person practicing emptiness; and one who is single-mindedly and constantly diligent in vigor is called a true practitioner of the Way. These three can reach nirvāṇa and attain the three gates of liberation, and so forth.
Regarding "the Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination," this next section praises the Truths and the Conditions.
These two have both similarities and differences: they are similar in that both involve Śrāvakas severing the afflictions of views and thought;
