first, an analysis according to the two truths; second, an elucidation of existence and non-existence; third, an analysis according to the six destinies; and fourth, an analysis according to the four castes.
This is the first point.

Above, it was clarified that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are conventional designations of phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti*); to reckon them as having a "sentient being" is a conventional designation of a person (*pudgala-prajñapti*).
From the perspective of worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they exist; from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they do not.
The section beginning with "whether existent or non-existent" clarifies existence and non-existence.
Non-Buddhists regard substantial reality as existence and vacuity as non-existence;
this is the root of the sixty-two views.
The passage beginning with "It merely gives rise to the mindfulness of sentient beings" explains the reason for its existence.

Ordinary people falsely reckon that there is a recipient, whereas the noble ones see sensation as being like an illusion or a transformation; this is entirely a contrast between the noble and the ordinary.
"Down to 'the six realms of existence'" (Section 3) explains the provisional nature of the aggregates (*skandha*) by means of the six destinies.
"'An illusory being seeing an illusory being'" (Section 4) explains it by means of the four castes.
What is called "viewing" refers to the illumination of the true as an illusory transformation and the illusory as a real transformation.
"True illusion" refers to the person of the Distinct Teaching (biejiao).
This clarifies the provisional nature of the recipient (*pratigrahaka*) in terms of both the transformer (*nirmāpaka*) and the transformed (*nirmita*).
Below the section "The Dharma of the Truth of Illusion," there are three explanations of provisional names.
The text has two parts:
first, clarifying that the Buddha knows the prior absence of names; second, clarifying that the Buddha establishes names for them.
The first section has three parts.
First, it clarifies names that lack corresponding referents.
This is because prior to the appearance of the Buddha in the world, there were no Great Sages to explain that names are merely conventional designations.
Below the phrase "illusory dharmas are illusory transformations," the second section clarifies that there is no substance corresponding to names.
Zhaokong says:
"Names lack the power to grasp things; things lack the reality to correspond to names."
"Below 'There are no three realms,' it clarifies that there are neither the three realms nor the six paths of existence.
"Below 'Therefore, Great King,' it clarifies the second point: the Buddha establishing names for them."
The text has two parts:
first, the Buddha establishes the name, which fully demonstrates that knowledge is provisional;
second, from "This is named Immeasurable" onwards, he concludes that the names are not singular.
Below the section on "the provisional nature of continuity" (*saṃtati-prajñapti*), the fourth part clarifies the provisional nature of continuity.
This text has three sections:
first, the statement of the thesis.
"Neither does the one continue," and so forth, is the second [part], the explanation.
Neither does the one continue because it is a single entity;
nor does the different continue because it is distinct.
"Neither identical nor different" concludes the third section on conformity.
This is like a sprout and its stem, which cannot be described as either identical or different.
"Dependent designation" concludes the fifth section, explaining dependent designation.
Within this passage there are two meanings:
all things that exist in mutual dependence are so by way of mutual exclusion.
As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "If a phenomenon is established through dependence, then that phenomenon itself becomes dependent."
"Phenomena such as the five colors and so forth are precisely relative.
Relativity is like the eye seeing color or the ear hearing sound.
If length and shortness are relative, this is relativity through mutual comparison."

"All dharmas are conventionally established through conditions," meaning that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and other such dharmas, acting as conditions, conventionally constitute sentient beings.
The section beginning with "the four fruits simultaneously" provides six explanations for the conventional arising from causes.
As with the five fruits and three causes, these constitute simultaneous cause and effect.
The two past causes and the five present fruits constitute asynchronous cause and effect.
Furthermore, the perception of conditions is simultaneous, while the observation of causes is asynchronous.
Furthermore, the rafters and beams that constitute a house exist simultaneously, whereas the twelve periods that constitute a day exist sequentially.
Moreover, the lamp and its light exist simultaneously, whereas darkness and light exist at different times.
"Everything is an illusion" and below, there are two sections concluding the provisional text;
this first concludes that the transformed [objects] are like illusions.
"Great King" and below, the second section clarifies that the transformer is like an illusion.
Because Bodhisattvas perceive sentient beings as unreal, like those with cataracts seeing flowers in the sky;
since sentient beings do not know this, [the Bodhisattvas] proclaim for them that all things are merely provisional designations.
This is the power and function of the Bodhisattva.
From the passage beginning with "At that time," the third section clarifies how the assembly gains benefit.
This section has two parts: [The text continues...]
First, the attainment of patience (*kṣānti*), which refers to the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) and those upon the grounds, up to the first ground.
Second, the virtues and conduct on the grounds.

Chapter Four: The Two Truths (*Dvayasatya*). Part One: Inner Protection (*adhyātmarakṣā*). This section contains three distinct parts; the present "Chapter on the Two Truths" is the third, clarifying the basis for the two types of protection.

Regarding the Two Truths, they constitute the great mainstay of the Buddha’s teaching. There are seven types: substantial existence, illusory existence, the separate entry into the common, the perfect entry into the common, the separate teaching, the perfect entry into the separate, and the perfect teaching; these are explained at length in the *Fahua Xuanyi* and other works.

It is simply because the perception of ordinary beings is shallow that it is called "conventional," while the perception of sages is profound that it is called "real"; because they are examined and verified, they are termed "truths" (*satya*).
Furthermore, the preceding "Chapter on Contemplating Emptiness" clarifies that both actual wisdom and skillful means are empty and are thus protected.

There are matters that those who have not yet attained realization must propagate through transformation; such transformation necessarily has its basis, namely the Two Truths, and it is for this reason that they are clarified here.
This chapter consists of two parts:
first, the questions and answers; second, the exhortation to uphold [the teaching].
The first section has three parts:
first, clarifying that the two truths are non-dual; second, clarifying that the teaching of the Dharma is non-dual; third, clarifying that the Dharma-gates are non-dual.
The first part has two sub-sections:
First the question, then the answer.
Within the question there are three parts:
first, the dual presentation of the topics.
From "At that time" onwards, two inquiries are raised in order to prepare for the upcoming objection.
Second, from "If one says it does not exist," the double refutation follows. Some say:
If one says they do not exist, then the wisdom of ordinary beings should not be twofold—namely, the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional.
If one says they do exist, then the wisdom of noble ones should not be singular; for that which is singular is the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
Now, it is said that if one asserts existence, one should not say that both existence and non-existence are empty; if one asserts non-existence, one should not differentiate between the two views.
The section beginning with "The meaning of 'one' and 'two'" concludes the three pairs.
From "The Buddha said to the Great King" onwards is the second response.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, the direct answer; second, the citation of scriptural evidence; and third, the explanation and establishment of the point.
The first section also has three parts:
first, praising Candraprabha’s past causes, which is easy to understand.
From "You now do not listen" onwards is the second part, the actual response.
To hear that all is empty is non-duality; to hear that they appear as they are is non-identity.
From "Listen attentively" (*tièng*) onwards, the three admonitions for listening encourage the cultivation of the three types of wisdom (*trividya*).
"Thus are the verses of the seven Buddhas," and so forth, marks the second section: the citation of scriptural evidence.
This verse consists of eight and a half lines, which are divided into three distinct parts:
the first three lines correctly set forth the two truths;
The next three lines explain the meaning, which constitutes the direct answer to the question;
the final two and a half lines conclude the preceding argument.
The first section has three parts:

The first line clarifies the two truths according to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*): the first half clarifies that the ultimate truth (*zhendi*) is both emptiness and existence, while the second half clarifies that the conventional truth (*suditi*) is both emptiness and existence.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "By whom were the twelve links of dependent origination created?"
The Buddha said:
"It is not made by a Buddha, nor by a Bodhisattva, nor even by any of the holy ones.
Therefore, it is said: "There is no self-made and no other-made."

From "The nature of dharmas is originally without nature" onwards, two sections of one line clarify the Two Truths of the Shared Teaching (*samdhāraśāsana*): the first half clarifies the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and the second half clarifies the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Regarding the "three provisional designations" (*tri-prajñapti*), these are the designation of dharmas, the designation of experience, and the designation of names.
Regarding the passage "There is no non-existence of the truth of reality" and below, the thirty-one lines clarify the two truths of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

Since there is no separate conventional truth, it is a single non-existence; since there is no separate ultimate truth, it is a single non-existence. Therefore, it is said that "there is no non-existence of the truth."
The first two lines clarify the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the next line clarifies the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and the final line provides a summary.
From "Existence and non-existence are fundamentally dual" onwards is the second part, the direct response to the objection, which clarifies that they are neither identical nor distinct.
The textual explanation has three parts: first, one verse clarifies the refutation of identity and difference through the mutual correspondence of wisdom and principle;
the first half of the verse elucidates oneness and duality, while the second half elucidates neither-identity-nor-difference, and so forth.

Regarding the passage "The mind of liberation sees non-duality" and below: the two lines of one verse contrast the principle of wisdom with [the object of] attachment to eliminate clinging. The first half clarifies that when the mind of liberation seeks duality, it is unattainable; the second half clarifies the elimination of attachment.
What is called "understanding" (jñāna) means seeing that both truths are empty.
Yet one then becomes attached to this emptiness; if even duality cannot be found, how could non-duality be found?

The passage beginning with "In understanding, there is always oneness" consists of three lines and one phrase, which praise the entry into the true meaning through the correspondence of principle and wisdom.
From "The conventional truth arises as an illusion" (*lokasatya-māyā-utpatti*) onwards, three and a half lines conclude the three preceding meanings.

The first line clarifies the three metaphors for existence and non-existence within the conventional truth: first, the metaphor of flowers in the sky; second, the metaphor of a reflection; and third, the metaphor of three hands.
"All are without reality," yet though they lack reality, they are not non-existent.
In the passage "An illusory transformation sees an illusory transformation" and below, two sections of one line each clarify the noble vision of existence and non-existence.
The second half-line, "Named the Contemplation of All Buddhas," establishes the correct contemplation.
From "Great King, Bodhisattva" onwards is the third section, which provides the explanation and establishment.
The commentary has two parts:
first, the clarification of two meanings; second, the clarification of one meaning.
Illuminating the conventional truth transforms ordinary beings; illuminating the ultimate truth transforms those of the Two Vehicles.
From "The Buddha and sentient beings" onwards, the second section clarifies the meaning of oneness.
This passage has three parts:
first, the clarification of the meaning of oneness through the mutual relation of subject and object, which is further divided into three: the thesis, the inquiry, and the explanation.
This is first, the initial statement.
"For what reason? is second, the inquiry.
From "Because sentient beings... onwards is the explanation.
"By means of the emptiness of sentient beings, one establishes the emptiness of bodhi" explains the Buddha’s capacity for transformation.
"By means of the emptiness of bodhi, one establishes the emptiness of sentient beings" explains those who are transformed.
Furthermore, the emptiness of sentient beings is the emptiness of persons, and the emptiness of bodhi is the emptiness of dharmas.
From the phrase "by means of all dharmas" onwards, two aspects—object and wisdom—are contrasted to clarify a single meaning.
The text has three parts: the heading, the inquiry, and the explanation.
Now, for the first:
"By means of all phenomena" refers to both object and wisdom, both of which are empty; therefore, it is called "emptiness of emptiness."
The phrase "For what reason? constitutes the second inquiry.
From the section "Prajñā is without marks" onwards, the explanation consists of two parts:
first, the direct explanation of one meaning, which is easily understood.
Next, following the passage "Prajñā is empty of ignorance," there are two sections that respond to objections and provide a further explanation. Why?
Because while all phenomena characterized by emptiness are manifest and can be known, what distinction is there in the emptiness of Prajñā?
Therefore, the present commentary states, "From ignorance up to the fruit of Buddhahood," in order to clarify the distinctions.
The text has two parts:
first, the clarification of the characteristics of emptiness according to the stages of delusion and awakening, which is easily understood.
Second, from "At the time of accomplishing the five eyes" onwards, the characteristics of emptiness are revealed in relation to the fruit of Buddhahood.
The text has two parts:
first, it clarifies seeing by means of non-seeing.
The four eyes, such as the flesh-eye and so forth, when present in a Buddha, are called the Buddha’s five eyes.
In the passage beginning with “Nor does he accept practice,” the second section clarifies practicing without practice, thereby departing from the five non-practices.
From "The Bodhisattva has not yet attained Buddhahood" onwards is the third section, which clarifies a single principle through the contrast between defilement and purity.
This section consists of three parts: the thesis, the inquiry, and the explanation.
The initial heading indicates what is to be seen.
"For what reason? is the interrogative inquiry.
The section beginning with "In the ultimate sense, it is non-dual" provides the threefold explanation.
Birth-and-death and bodhi are like light and darkness; although they appear as two, in emptiness they are not two.
From the passage "He addressed the Buddha," the second section clarifies that the teaching of the Dharma is non-dual.
The text has two parts:
first, the question; second, the answer.
The intent of the question is as follows:
"If all emptinesses are suchness (tathatā), they are devoid of words and letters; for what reason, then, do the sages employ them for the purpose of teaching?
The passage beginning with "The Great King’s Wheel of Dharma" provides the answer.
The text has two parts:
first, clarifying the teaching of emptiness; second, clarifying the cultivation of emptiness.
The first part has three sections:
First, it is clarified that "name" is empty.
Regarding what is called the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra), there are generally two kinds:
first, practice; second, teaching.
The "Dharmapada" refers to the Sūtra-piṭaka;
the "Repetition" refers to the Geya-piṭaka;
and the "Prophecy" refers to the Vyākaraṇa-piṭaka.
"Those not recited as verses and sūtras" refers to the Gāthā-sūtras.
"Spontaneous utterances without being questioned" refers to the Udāna-sūtras.
"Disciplinary codes" refers to the Nidāna-sūtras.
"Parable" (aupamya) refers to the *Avadāna* sūtras.
"Dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu) refers to the *Itivṛttaka* sūtras; the *Mahāsūtra* calls them the *Śīla-sūtra*.
"Vetulya" refers to the Sūtras of Jātaka;
"Vaipulya" refers to the Vaipulya Sūtras;
and "Adbhutadharma" refers to the Adbhutadharma Sūtras.
“Discourse” (vāda) refers to the *Upadeśa* sūtras.
These twelve are all empty, which is precisely suchness (*tathatā*).
In the passage beginning with “These names, phrases, and syllables,” the second point clarifies the emptiness of the teaching.
Using the sounds and voices of this land as a Buddha-work, because the nature of written characters is free from [inherent existence], they are all thusness (*tathatā*).
The section beginning with "If one grasps at written characters" clarifies the third point: the non-practice of emptiness.
To practice emptiness in this manner is not right contemplation.
From the passage "Great King, suchness is a mere word" onwards, the second section clarifies the cultivation of emptiness.
This section has three parts:
First, the analysis of cultivation is twofold: first,
clarifying the stage of the cause.
Because wisdom arises from the teaching, the teaching is the mother of wisdom.
Furthermore, emptiness is like letters and letters are like emptiness; therefore, it is called "suchness" (*tathatā*).
Because this suchness can give rise to the Buddha-wisdom, it is called the "mother of wisdom."
Below the phrase “all sentient beings,” the second section clarifies the stage of fruition:
when present within the bodies of sentient beings, it is called Buddha-nature; when present within the body of a Buddha, it is named the Knowledge of All Modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Before attaining Buddhahood, one will certainly attain it; because one is destined to attain it, one is called the "Mother-to-be.
Before the Way is attained, it is called Buddha-nature; once the Way is attained, it is called the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Regarding 'The Prajñā of the Three Vehicles' below, this is the second section, which provides a further explanation in response to difficulties.

This means that because it was previously stated that [Prajñā] is the mother of the Buddha's wisdom, and again that it is the mother of the fundamental wisdom of nature, there was concern that people might find this difficult to understand; therefore, it is now explained once more."
The explanation has two parts:
first, the explanation of the nature of principle; second, the explanation of the nature of practice. Principle is the mother of the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā*).
Now, for the first part, the explanation of the nature of principle refers to the aforementioned mother of fundamental wisdom.
The passage beginning with "If a bodhisattva... explains below, through the nature of the two practices, that suchness-wisdom is the mother [of all].
If a bodhisattva studies without words and cultivates without cultivation, they immediately attain true wisdom, which is *prajñā*.
From "Great King, if a bodhisattva... onwards is the third section, which concludes the cultivation and accomplishment.
Next, from "He addressed the Buddha, saying... onwards is the third part, clarifying the non-duality of the dharma-gate; it first presents the question and subsequently provides the answer.
In the questions, there are three parts:
the first is the question regarding the faculties;
"the practices are also immeasurable" is the second question regarding the practices.
The passage beginning with "The Dharma-gate is one" constitutes three questions regarding the Dharma-gate.
Furthermore, the intent of the question is as follows:
since the faculties, natures, and dispositions of sentient beings differ, are the contemplative gates taught by them one or two?
From "Great King" onwards, the two Buddhas provide the answer.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, a brief answer; second, an extensive answer; and finally, a concluding answer.
The first section has two parts:
first, the explanation of the gate of contemplation; second, the explanation of the phenomena to be contemplated.
Now, the first part is easily understood.
"Furthermore, all phenomena are not characterized by existence," and so forth; this second section clarifies the phenomena that are the objects of observation.
They are "not characterized by existence" because their characteristics are unreal.
They are "not non-characterized by non-existence" because they are free from the error of nihilism.
"Regarding 'If a bodhisattva' and below, there is a second part: the detailed explanation and response.
This text has three sections;
the first clarifies [the meaning] by means of the two truths."

"Regarding the passage 'If a bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings' and below: the two [distinctions] are conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); not seeing one or two is ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Because the conventional is itself emptiness, it is said that non-duality is the ultimate truth;
the existence or non-existence of things is the root of all views and is termed worldly truth (*loka-satya*)."
Regarding the section beginning with "By means of the three truths," the second part explains all phenomena by way of the three truths. Some say:
emptiness is the Truth (the ultimate reality), form refers to the five sense organs, and mind refers to the six consciousnesses.
Now, when we speak of "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*), both principle and phenomena are encompassed.

Regarding emptiness: from space up to *prajñā*, there are both the conventional and the ultimate. Regarding form: from substantial form up to true form, there are also both the conventional and the ultimate. Regarding mind: from the arising and ceasing up to the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*), there are likewise both the conventional and the ultimate. Thus, the inclusion of phenomena is truly vast.
The five kinds of the three truths are as explained in the *Fahua xuanyi*.
In the section beginning with "self, person, knowledge, and vision," the three [truths] are manifested through the three types of provisional designation (*prajñapti*).

"Self, person, knowledge, and vision" is the provisional designation of names; the five aggregates (*skandhas*) are the provisional designation of receiving; and all phenomena (*dharmas*) are the provisional designation of dharmas.
Below "The Chapter on Sentient Beings" are the three concluding responses.
Below "The Seven Buddhas, Great King," is the second major section: Encouraging Retention.
This text has two parts:
First, praising the teaching; second, citing the name to encourage its upholding.
The first section has five parts:
the first clarifies that the teaching is identical to that of the seven Buddhas, which is easy to understand.
The section beginning with "You, the great assembly" constitutes the second part, which cites the benefits and exhorts one to uphold [the teaching].
The section beginning with "How much more so in this case" constitutes the third part, which clarifies superior faith.
To be able to believe in this sutra is to accomplish the three types of wisdom, thereby transcending the merits of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).
"Furthermore, as for those who uphold [this teaching]," the following four points clarify their attainment of entry.
According to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), one attains Buddhahood at the first stage (Chuzhu) and is able to transform sentient beings throughout a hundred Buddha-worlds.
From "At that time, the great assembly... onwards, there is the fifth section: the benefits obtained. From "Great King, this sutra...
onwards, there is the second section: citing the light to encourage its upholding.
This section has two parts:
First, the names are raised for clarification.
From "Also named 'All'" onwards, the second section clarifies the function, which is evident.

Chapter Five: Protecting the Nation. Regarding the fifth chapter, "Protecting the Nation," there are four parts to the formal exposition. The first three chapters have completed the explanation of internal protection; now, this "Protecting the Nation" chapter is the second part, clarifying external protection.
There are two kinds of lands:
first, the mundane, which includes those of the Two Vehicles and ordinary beings;
second, the supramundane, which extends from the ten levels of faith up to the ten bhūmis.
There are two kinds of thieves:
first, external ones such as robbers; second, internal ones consisting of the afflictions and fetters.
There are likewise two kinds of protection:
The first is the external, namely the spirits and deities within a hundred paces;
the second is the internal, which is wisdom.
Whether internal or external, these are all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, gods, and spirits capable of protecting the lands of people; therefore, it is named the "Chapter on Protecting the State."

In terms of contemplation: one contemplates the phenomena of arising and ceasing to protect the Land of Co-residence; one contemplates the phenomena of non-arising and non-ceasing to protect the Land of Remainder; one contemplates immeasurable phenomena to protect the Land of Retribution; and one contemplates the unconditioned phenomena to protect the Land of Tranquil Light.
Furthermore, the spirits and deities protect the country as its *paribhoga* (enjoyment) support; the practice of *prajñāpāramitā* protects the country as its *vipākaphala* (retribution) support.
Moreover, the spirits and deities protect life and so forth.
From the passage "At that time, the Buddha addressed the Great King" onwards, the text of this chapter is divided into three parts:
First, the exhortation to listen and uphold; second, the extensive explanation; third, the clarification of the benefits for the assembly.
Regarding the first, the text is easily understood.
From the passage beginning with "When the land is about to fall into chaos," the second part follows: the extensive explanation of protecting the Dharma.

The text has three parts: first, a detailed explanation of protecting the Dharma; second, citing antiquity to corroborate the present; third, concluding with an exhortation to uphold it. The first part has three sections: 1. A detailed explanation of protecting the Dharma; 2. Citing antiquity to corroborate the present; 3. Concluding with an exhortation to uphold it.
The first section has three parts: [as specified above].
First, protection of the state; second, protection of merit; third, protection from calamities.
The first section has four parts: first, protection of time; second, protection of the Dharma; third, protection of the essence; fourth, revealing the calamities protected against.
This is the first [case].
Since the king’s mind does not fear when there is no calamity, but fears only when a calamity occurs, this clarifies the "time.
Furthermore, actual harm is taken as "burning," which does not necessarily refer to the time of a fire disaster.
From "When one requests a hundred Buddhas" onwards, the second section clarifies the protection of the Dharma.
This text has three parts:
first, it clarifies the field of merit; second, it clarifies the offerings; and third, it clarifies the time for preaching.
The initial section further divides into three parts:
first, the invitation of the worthy and holy ones.
Since their true bodies are difficult to behold, physical images are established to manifest the ritual of reverence.
Below the phrase "a multitude of one hundred bhikṣus," the second section clarifies the audience.
These consist of the fourfold assembly of devas, nāgas, humans, and pretas.

Furthermore, there are the fourfold assemblies of those who are the primary recipients of the teaching (the *dharmabhājana*), those with whom a karmic connection is established (*pratyaya-bandha*), those who initiate the teaching (*pravartaka*), and those who act as responsive echoes (*pratibimba*).
The "seven assemblies" consist of the five assemblies of those who have left the household life: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās.
"The two groups of householders" refers to the laymen and laywomen of pure faith.
"Requesting one hundred Dharma masters" and below indicates the threefold invitation for the masters to preach.
"One hundred lion's roars" and below clarifies the second section: making offerings.
The text has three parts:
first, there are three methods of offering, namely lamps, flowers, and incense;
following "the three robes," second, there is the offering to the Dharma Master.
"Personal belongings" refers to: 1. the three robes; 2. the alms bowl; 3. the sitting mat; 4. the razor; 5. the small knife; 6. the water-strainer; 7. the bowl bag; 8. and the needle case.
"Under 'a small amount of rice,' the three types of food offerings are clarified.
Under 'one day of the Great King,' the three times for preaching are clarified.
Under 'within your kingdom,' the third point clarifies the protector, which is the essence of protection."
In the *Suvarṇākṣa-ṛṣi-artha-sūtra* from foreign lands, it is stated that there are ten fundamental spirits (*bhūta*), each of which is further divided into ten, making one hundred.

These are: first, the Great Deity; second, the Youthful Deity; third, the Mother Deity; fourth, the Brahma Deity; fifth, the Crane-headed Deity; sixth, the Nāga Deity; seventh, the Asura; eighth, the Śa Deity; ninth, the Yakṣa Deity; and tenth, the Rākṣasa Deity.

"During the time of turmoil in the Great King’s realm," and below, the fourth section clarifies the difficulties to be protected against. The text has three parts; the first clarifies the difficulties caused by ghosts and humans, which comprise eight [subsections]: 1. The difficulty of being born as a hungry ghost (*preta*). 2. The difficulty of being born as a human. 3. The difficulty of being born in a border region. 4. The difficulty of having defective faculties. 5. The difficulty of holding wrong views. 6. The difficulty of being born in a world where a Buddha has not appeared. 7. The difficulty of being born at a time when the True Dharma has ceased. 8. The difficulty of encountering a false teacher. [The text continues: "First, the difficulty of being born as a hungry ghost. This refers to those who, due to their past karma, are born in the realm of hungry ghosts and suffer from hunger and thirst. Furthermore, there are two types of hungry ghosts: those who roam in the air and those who dwell on the earth. Those who roam in the air are further divided into three categories: those who eat filth, those who eat fire, and those who eat wind. Those who dwell on the earth are also divided into three categories: those who eat excrement, those who eat vomit, and those who eat pus and blood. These are collectively called the eight classes of hungry ghosts. Because they are constantly tormented by hunger and thirst, they have no leisure for the practice of the Way; therefore, this is called a "difficulty. "Second, the difficulty of being born as a human. Although birth as a human is superior to birth as a hungry ghost, it is still considered a difficulty because one may be born in a state of suffering. There are four types of such suffering: first, the suffering of poverty and lack; second, the suffering of being oppressed by others; third, the suffering of being born in a border region; and fourth, the suffering of having defective faculties. Because these beings are unable to encounter the Buddha-Dharma, this is called a "difficulty. "Third, the difficulty of being born in a border region. Border regions refer to places where the teachings of the Buddha have not spread, or where the customs are contrary to the Dharma. Because one cannot hear the sublime Dharma in such places, this is called a "difficulty. "Fourth, the difficulty of having defective faculties. Defective faculties refer to those who are blind, deaf, mute, or mentally impaired. Because their physical or mental organs are incomplete, they are unable to perceive the Buddha-Dharma; therefore, this is called a "difficulty. "Fifth, the difficulty of holding wrong views. Holding wrong views means rejecting the principle of cause and effect and adhering to heterodox paths. Because such individuals turn away from the true path, this is called a "difficulty. "Sixth, the difficulty of being born in a world where a Buddha has not appeared. This refers to aeons in which no Buddha has arisen in the world. Without a Buddha to teach the Dharma, there is no way to attain liberation; therefore, this is called a "difficulty. "Seventh, the difficulty of being born at a time when the True Dharma has ceased. Even if a Buddha has appeared, if the True Dharma has already vanished, there is no teaching to rely upon. Because the opportunity for practice is lost, this is called a "difficulty. "Eighth, the difficulty of encountering a false teacher. A false teacher is one who claims to teach the Dharma but instead preaches heterodoxy, leading sentient beings astray. Because this obstructs the attainment of the right path, this is called a "difficulty. Thus, these eight types of difficulties are collectively termed the "difficulties of ghosts and humans. One must protect oneself against them so as not to fall into such states. Therefore, the text says: "If one can avoid these eight difficulties, one will surely be able to meet with a Buddha and hear the Dharma. This concludes the first part.

First, the chaos of ghosts; second, the chaos of the people; third, the arrival of bandits; fourth, the death and loss of the common folk; fifth, disputes between ruler and minister; sixth, strange anomalies in heaven and earth; seventh, the constellations losing their proper courses; eighth, the sun and moon losing their proper courses.

Regarding the twenty-eight lunar mansions, the "Chapter on Gathering and Sustaining" (*Mahāsaṃnipāta-saṃgraha-parivarta*) states: "In the east are seven stars: Jyeṣṭhā (角), Kṛttikā (亢), Rohiṇī (氐), Mṛgaśiras (房), Puṣya (心), Āśleṣā (尾), and Maghā (箕)."
The seven lunar mansions of the south are Jing, Gui, Liu, Xing, Zhang, Yi, and Zhen.
The seven lunar mansions of the west are Kui, Lou, Wei, Mao, Bi, Zi, and Shen.
"The seven lunar mansions of the north are Dou (Dipper), Niu (Ox), Nu (Woman), Xu (Void), Wei (Danger), Shi (Room), and Bi (Wall).
"If the Great King encounters the calamity of fire" refers below to the second or third types of disasters.

According to this text, the primary requirement is simply to provide the lecture.
"Great King, not only do you protect merit," and so forth; the following three sections explain the protection against various calamities.
Regarding the "four grave offenses": they are sexual misconduct, theft, killing, and lying.
The "five heinous offenses" (*pañcānantarya*) are: killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, causing a schism in the Sangha, killing an Arhat, and shedding the blood of a Buddha.

The "eight difficulties" (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*) are: first, the hells; second, the animal realm; third, the realm of hungry ghosts; fourth, the long-lived heavens; fifth, the borderlands; sixth, the impairment of the sense faculties; seventh, false views; and eighth, not seeing a Buddha.
"Great King, in the past there was a king... and so forth. This is the second section, which cites ancient precedents to corroborate the present.

first, citing celestial beings to prove protection of the state; second, citing human kings to prove protection of the person.
This is the first [chapter].
The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Xiányújīng*) states: "In a past age, there was a great kingdom with a king named Śubhavyūha (Good Abiding).
At that time, a tumor suddenly grew upon his crown, shaped like a cocoon; though it was removed, he felt no pain."
As he grew larger and larger, he eventually became a youth who was exceedingly handsome, with deep blue-black hair and a body the color of purple-gold.

He immediately summoned a physiognomist, who prophesied that the child possessed the virtues of a noble king and would surely rule over the four quarters; thus, he was given the name Mūrdhaja (Top-Born).
As the years passed, he grew up and his virtue became renowned.
When his father, the king, passed away, the various kings, ministers, and others requested that he be entrusted with the throne.
Mūrdhaja replied:
"I shall only ascend the throne once my karmic merit has brought about the response of kingship, such that the Four Heavenly Kings and Śakra come to welcome me.
Having completed this vow, the Four Heavenly Kings descended, each holding a precious vase filled with fragrant water to pour over his crown.
Then Śakra, Lord of Devas, again brought a jeweled crown and fashioned it into a canopy for him.
He indulged in the five desires of Jambudvīpa for eighty-four thousand years.

Then, a yakṣa spirit emerged from the earth and invited him to travel to Pūrvavideha for eight hundred million years; he was further invited to Aparagoyānī for one hundred and forty million years, and then ascended to the Heaven of the Four Great Kings for another one hundred and forty million years.

In his mind, he further thought of ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; five hundred rishis supported the chariot as they flew together into the heavens. From afar, he beheld the royal city, which had one thousand two hundred gates; seeing that all the gods were terrified, he heard that heavy bolts had been fastened to every gate.
Māndhātṛ’s army advanced directly toward it without obstruction; as they blew conch shells and struck lutes, the twelve hundred gates opened simultaneously.

Śakra immediately emerged to meet them and invited them into the palace to share his throne. While enjoying sensual pleasures in the heavens, Māndhātṛ again went outside and blew his conch shell and struck his bow.
Once the evil mind had arisen, he consequently fell [from his celestial state]; subsequently afflicted by a malignant disease, he then met his death.
He who was Śakra at that time was Kāśyapa Buddha.
"As for the one called Mūrdhaja, he is my current self.

According to this sutra, at that time the Lord of Devas prepared a hundred high seats like those used by the Buddhas of the Seven [Buddha] Periods and invited a hundred Dharma masters to lecture and recite this sutra; thereupon, Mūrdhaja immediately retreated.

"Great King, in the past there was a king named Tārā... and so forth. This section has two parts: first, citing a human king as a witness to protect the body; second, the text itself, which consists of two sections:

Regarding the first point:

the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states, "In the past, King Pramoda entered the mountains with his fourfold army to hunt; there he encountered a female lion who yielded her desire to the king."
When the lioness’s gestation was complete, she gave birth to a male child whose entire body resembled that of a human, while his spotted feet resembled those of his mother.
The lioness carried her son back to the king’s presence; the king took him as his own son and gave him the name Pāṇḍu (Spotted Foot).
This king constantly made offerings to a single rishi, perpetually providing him with pure food.
One day, when the rishi did not come to the king’s presence, a celestial deity manifested as a rishi and entered the royal palace to seek fish and meat.
The former seer returned at the appointed hour; when the king offered him meat, the seer grew indignant and, as a result, uttered this curse:
"In twelve years hence, you shall constantly eat human flesh."
When the seer had finished speaking, he returned to the mountains.

Thereafter, the chief cook was unable to prepare the meal as required; going outside, he saw no meat, but seeing a dead infant, he hurriedly took its flesh, prepared food with it, and presented it to the king.
The king found the food exceedingly delicious and immediately asked about its origin.
The cook answered in detail,
and the king said:
"From this day forward, you shall use this flesh.
Thereafter, the cook constantly captured small children and killed them to provide food for the king, serving him every day.
When the people of the country lost their children, they searched everywhere until they saw the cook capturing other small children.
The cook was seized and bound, and the people of the country informed the king.
The king said,
"I commanded it."
The people of the country all said, "This is a great thief; he lies in wait by the king's bathing pool with hidden soldiers to seize the king.
Once the king was captured, he immediately addressed the people:
"I pray you grant me one pardon, and I shall never kill again."
The people of the kingdom would not permit it, so the king immediately made this vow:
"May all the various merits I have cultivated since birth be redirected so that today I may instead become a flying rākṣasa who devours humans."
Having spoken thus, he immediately vanished into the air and proclaimed:
"From this day forward, you shall eat the wives and children whom you love.
Upon hearing this, the people fled in haste.
Many rākṣasas became attached to him and followed him, so that his retinue gradually grew large and the harm he caused became increasingly widespread.
Later, the rākṣasas said:
"We shall now act according to the command of our King; we must seize a thousand kings for our kind and hold a great assembly."
Pāṇḍu said, "Very well.
He went to fetch them one by one until he had obtained nine hundred and ninety-nine kings; he was lacking only one king, for which reason he could not hold the assembly.
The kings each said,
"Today we have no one to whom we may turn for refuge.
If we could capture King Sudāsa, he possesses great skillful means and could save our lives."
Having formed this plan, he said to Pāṇḍu:
"The King wishes to hold a great assembly.
King Śuddhodana possesses great fame and virtue; if that king could come, the assembly would be made perfect."
Then the Rākṣasa king immediately went in haste to seize him.
At that time, King Sudāsa was leaving the city for the garden and entering the pond to bathe; he saw the beggar following behind the king.
The king said, "Wait until I have finished bathing and then I shall give it to you.
As soon as the king entered the pool, the Rākṣasa king descended invisibly from the air and seized him; Sudāsa was then filled with grief and wept piteously.
King Pāṇḍu said, "I have heard that you are the foremost of men in fame and virtue;
why do you weep? King Suda said:
"I do not cherish my own body or life.
This morning I went out and saw a beggar and intended to give to him; however, I encountered the King and returned, failing to go through with it.
It is for this reason that I am grieving."
"I pray that Your Majesty will grant me seven days to bestow alms upon the practitioners of the Way.
Bandhula granted the king's request to return for seven days to bestow alms upon the practitioners of the Way.

At that time, the Brahmin recited a verse for the king, identical to that in this sutra; hearing it, the king was filled with joy and immediately installed his crown prince to take over the throne. He then took leave of his ministers and went to his death.
King Pāṇḍu said, "You are now facing death; why are you so joyful?
Sudatta replied:
“The Great King’s grace is vast; grant me seven days to bestow alms upon the practitioners of the Way, so that by hearing the subtle and wondrous Dharma, my mind may attain spontaneous understanding.
Thus shall my vow be fulfilled. Bandhumat asked:
"What Dharma have you heard?
Suṭa immediately proclaimed the sublime Dharma for him, and further explained the retribution for the sin of killing.
Having heard this, Bandhumat immediately released Suṭa and the various kings, each of whom returned to their own kingdoms.

Question:
Since the mountain is large and the mustard seed is small, how can he enter it?
Answer:
Some say he entered by means of the Buddha’s supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). Others say:
The mustard seed and the mountain are both "as such" (tathatā), and thus they interpenetrate as they are.
Furthermore, some say: "The three realms are mind-only.
Here, the mind is likened to the mustard seed and the three realms to the mountain; because the mind is able to create the realms, it is called "entering."
Some say: "Mountains and mustard seeds both do not exist; because phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are empty, and because they are empty, they can interpenetrate.

Now I say: if one explains this by means of emptiness, then when one is empty, all are empty. Both the mountain and the mustard seed are empty, and because they are empty, they are able to interpenetrate.
All are conventionally designated; both the mountain and the mustard seed are conventionally designated. Because they are conventionally designated, their mutual inclusion is discussed.
All are central; both the mountain and the mustard seed are central. Because they are central, their mutual inclusion is discussed.
When emptiness removes views and afflictions, it is *prajñā*; when the provisional removes ignorance, it is liberation; when the middle removes nescience, it is the *dharmakāya*.
Thus, they are three while being one, and one while being three—like the three eyes of the celestial being, neither vertical nor horizontal; this is called the inconceivable one.

the concluding praise.

Answer:
The *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra* states: "Śākyamuni Buddha is named Vairocana.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "He is also named Śākya and also named Śāna."
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "This body of mine is now the Dharmakāya.
Vairocana means "Pure and Full" (Jingman); "Pure" refers to the Jewel.
Question:
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states that "Vairocana is the root"; why, then, do you now say that Śākyamuni is the root?
Answer:
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* clarifies the traces and the fundamental; this sūtra clarifies the fundamental and the traces.
Although the fundamental and the traces differ, they are one in their inconceivability.
Question:
How does this sutra differ from the "Jeweled Stupa" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?
Answer:
There are both similarities and differences.
What is the same is that both equally clarify Śākyamuni as the fundamental source.
What is different is that this sutra retains expedient means, whereas the *Lotus Sūtra* is direct and abandons expedient means.

The meaning of the answer is that one attains this path only by explaining it through the practice of seeking the supreme above while transforming those below;
although there are many ways to open up the emptiness [of this path], three types will be briefly explained.
If form is itself emptiness, it opens up the knowledge of all modes;
if emptiness is itself form, it opens up the knowledge of the paths;
if form and emptiness are non-dual, it opens up the knowledge of all aspects.

If form were not empty, there would be the delusion of views and afflictions; if emptiness were not form, there would be the delusion of ignorance; and if the Middle Way were not attained, there would be the delusion of nescience.
These three are all gateways; thus, these three contemplations are the opening of the three wisdoms. This is the general outline.

*upāsikā* refers to a female lay follower.
Below the phrase "Practicing the Ten Wholesome Deeds," the text explains the practice of the three types of knowledge (*vidyā*).
This section has three parts:
first, the cultivation of the ten wholesome practices; this refers to the ten wholesome deeds, which are identical to the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*).
"Observing one's own body" and below, there are two parts concerning the cultivation of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
First, one contemplates the six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*); next, one contemplates the sense faculties (*indriya*); and finally, one contemplates the three realms (*tridhātu*).
"The five feelings" refers to the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).
"The five sensations" refer to suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity.
Regarding the phrase "dwelling in the Buddha's family," it means that from the third life onward, one is born into the Buddha's family and practices the six points of harmonious respect.
"Good son, practicing patience" and below, the fourth section uses the inferior to illustrate the superior.
The text has two parts:
first, citing the inferior; second, illustrating the superior by comparison.
The first section has two parts:
first, the direct explanation of the inferior stage, which can be understood through the dharma, the metaphor, and the application.
From "Although for ten thousand kalpas" onwards, the second part addresses and overcomes potential objections.
The commentary has two parts:

first, raising and resolving the objection; second, the explanation [beginning with] "yet it cannot be named. Regarding the question, "How can it be said that there is both regression and progress in the stage of patience?"—this is the first part. The second part is the explanation.
The penetrations (*abhisamaya*) are threefold and cannot be named; therefore, there is regression.
From the passage "As for those who have attained this concentration" (*yaḥ samādhi-lābhī*) onwards, the second section reveals their superior status.
This section consists of two parts:
First, regarding "attainment":

this refers to Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) who, for the first time, realize the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and attain the nature of the noble ones (*ārya-gotra*); therefore, it is called "concentration" (*samādhi*).

This differs from the preceding stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), which is not yet fixed, because during the ten faiths one has not yet attained liberation and practices exclusively the contemplation of entering emptiness through the provisional (*prajñapti*).
"Will certainly not commit the five heinous crimes" and below, the second section clarifies the avoidance of transgressions.
This section has four parts:

first, not committing the five heinous crimes; second, not committing the six grave offenses; third, not committing the twenty-eight light offenses; and fourth, not slandering the Buddha-dharma or its scriptures.
The initial passage is clear.
Regarding the "six grave offenses," as stated in the fourth fascicle of the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, in the chapter on "Receiving the Precepts":
first, killing; second, stealing; third, sexual misconduct; fourth, lying; fifth, selling liquor; and sixth, speaking of the faults of the fourfold assembly of monastics and laypeople.
Regarding the "Twenty-eight Minor Transgressions," they are as explained in the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*:
first, failing to provide offerings to one's parents, teachers, and elders; second, being habitually addicted to alcohol; third, being unable to attend to those suffering from illness;
fourth, being unable to practice even small acts of giving and charity; fifth, failing to rise to greet and pay homage upon seeing the fourfold assembly.
Sixth, seeing the fourfold assembly violating the precepts, one gives rise to arrogance;
seventh, being unable each month to observe the eight precepts and make offerings to the Triple Gem; eighth, not listening when there is a lecture within forty *li*;
ninth, accepting bedding, seats, or couches belonging to the *caitya* Saṃgha; tenth, drinking water because one suspects it contains insects; eleventh, traveling alone through dangerous places.
12. Staying alone in a nunnery; 13. Beating or scolding servants and others for the sake of wealth or one's life;
14. Giving leftover food to the fourfold assembly; 15. Keeping cats or ferrets; 16.

Keeping elephants, horses, or any other domestic animals without having made them a pure gift (*pariṣkāra*) to those who have not yet received the precepts; 17. Hoarding extra robes or alms bowls beyond the permitted limit.
18. Working as a field laborer; 19. Selling goods with dishonest measures or scales;
20. Engaging in sexual desire at improper times; 21. Failing to pay taxes to the king; 22. Violating the laws of the state; 23.
Upon obtaining new fruits or vegetables, failing to offer them to the Triple Gem; 24. If the Sangha does not permit [the teaching], one should not preach.
Twenty-five: To walk upon the twenty-five-fold roads ahead of all renunciants; twenty-six:
To act as a teacher to one’s elders throughout the communal meal; twenty-seven: To raise silkworms; twenty-eight:
Upon encountering a sick person on the road, to fail to stop and attend to them, but instead entrust them to others and depart.
"Regarding 'the Buddhist scriptures' below, [this refers to] the fourth [point]: not slandering the Buddhist scriptures by claiming they were not spoken by the Buddha.

Regarding "the eradication of the ten inversions": the four foundations of mindfulness eliminate the four inversions; the three wholesome roots eliminate the three poisons; and the contemplation of the three periods of time eliminates fixed attachment to the three periods.
The "self, person, knowledge, and vision" are merely conventional designations established upon phenomena and are not real.

The section beginning with "By two asaṃkhyeyas" indicates the duration of time for entering the three stages.
"Bharadvāja" means "guardian. The practices of the Bodhisattva of the Ten Practices are firm and stable;

"Furthermore, regarding the 'Path-knowledge' (mārgajñatā)," and so forth, the third section clarifies the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Dedications (daśapariṇāmanā).
The text has three parts:
first, the designation of the stage.
Because they cultivate the correct contemplation of the Middle Way, it is called the "nature of the modes of the path" (*mārgākāra-gotra*).
Below the phrase "abiding in firm endurance," there are two sections that distinguish the differences.
The text has two parts:
First, the distinctions among contemplations are clarified:

by contemplating the five aggregates of grasping, one attains the fivefold Dharma-body; by contemplating the three realms, one attains the three emptinesses; and by contemplating the two truths, one attains the two patiences of impermanence and non-arising.
The tenth is "the ultimate truth" (*paramārthasatya*), which is the emptiness of the Middle Way of non-arising.
From the phrase "yet taking birth in the three realms" onwards, there are two [sections] concerning the excellence of receiving retribution.
The prose section has three parts:
first, the heading, which is easily understood;
second, the inquiry, "For what reason? (kasmāt).
"Since the mind has already attained quiescence, how can there be rebirth?
Regarding the phrase "the fruit of karmic habituation," there are three explanations.

Because one has not yet ascended to the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*), one is still permeated by the ignorance that has not been severed; since views and attachments (*dṛṣṭi-rāga*) still persist, rebirth occurs.

The passage beginning with "Furthermore, by three asaṃkhyeya kalpas" below refers to the duration of time for entering the stages; it takes that much time of cultivation before one attains the first bhūmi.
Because one simultaneously illuminates the two truths, they are called "equal sages."
Because one does not regress at this stage, it is called "avaivartika" (non-retrogressive).

The text consists of five parts.
First is the designation of the stage, which is clear from the text itself.
From "Abiding in the patience of equality" (*samatākṣānti*) onwards is the second part, which distinguishes the differences in practice.
The text has two parts:
first, it clarifies that the two wisdoms constitute the characteristics; second, it reveals the similarities and differences between the two wisdoms.
The first part has two sections:
First, the headings are presented; second, they are explained in detail.
Regarding the first, "Equal Endurance" (*samatākṣānti*), this indicates actual wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*), which simultaneously illuminates both existence and non-existence without being defiled by them.
The phrase "the four means of integration" (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*) and so forth indicates the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).
The section beginning with "entering signlessness, equanimity, and cessation" provides two distinct explanations.
This text consists of two parts:
First, the wisdom of the true mark (*dharmatā-jñāna*) is explained, followed by the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).
The initial section has three parts:
first, a general enumeration; second, a detailed explanation; and third, the clarification of the transcendence of marks.
Regarding the first point, the text is clear.
From the phrase "In the ultimate truth" (*paramārthasatya*) onwards, there are two distinct explanations.
The text consists of three parts:
First, "the unconditioned nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā-asamskṛta*), which is also called "the unconditioned of space" (*ākāśa-asamskṛta*).
Second, "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asamskṛta*), which refers to that which is extinguished by relying on principle;
it is the unconditioned of signlessness (*animitta-asamskṛta*) wherein the Buddha’s true wisdom extinguishes all fetters (*saṃyojana*).

"Abiding in the first stage of patience" (*kṣānti*) refers below to the three unconditioned states (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) that are not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), namely the dharmas such as signlessness (*animitta*).
"The unconditioned of signlessness" and so forth below clarify the three ways of being free from the two signs of existence and non-existence.
Below "Immeasurable Expedient Means," the second section reveals the wisdom of expedient means.
This passage has two parts:
the first is the heading, which is easy to understand.

Regarding the section beginning with "The skillful means of the true nature (bhūtalakṣaṇa)," there are two explanations. There are six kinds of skillful means: first, the skillful means of the true nature;

second, the skillful means of universal study; third, the skillful means of dedication (pariṇāmanā); fourth, the skillful means of mastery; fifth, the skillful means of the One Vehicle (ekayāna); and sixth, the skillful means of transformation, and so forth.
"Thus, good son," and so forth, is the second section, which provides a double explanation of the similarities and differences between the two types of wisdom.
This passage has three parts;
first, concluding the preceding discussion on their differing characteristics, it first clarifies the characteristics of ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
Because it is the initial awakening to the Middle Way, it is called "the wisdom of initial awakening.
The passage beginning with "Skillfully employing without realization" describes the characteristics of the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).
The section beginning with "For example" provides two analogies to clarify what is not [the case], demonstrating that they are neither identical nor distinct.
Regarding the phrase "and each and every practice is accomplished," this refers to the accomplishment of the three practices.

Because one attains that which is simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle, a single practice becomes immeasurable practices and immeasurable practices become a single practice; therefore, it is said they are "accomplished."
"By attaining the four reliances," etc., the third section clarifies the timing.
Because the perfection of giving is realized upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), it is said: "Entering the gate of the treasury of merit."
"Having no karma for the three realms" refers to being reborn next in the Pure Lands, namely the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder and the Land of True Reward.
"Constantly practicing the contemplation of equanimity" refers to the fifth stage, ascending to the position.
Because he cultivates equanimity (*upekṣā*), he attains the fulfillment of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
"Kumāra" means "Victor over Enemies," because he has abandoned the enemies of the three realms and the two vehicles.
Regarding the "Four Treasuries," some say they consist of the Tripitaka and the Miscellaneous Treasury (Kṣudraka-piṭaka).
For now, we shall rely solely on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*:
First is the priceless treasury, which is the Bodhisattva Vehicle;
second is the high-priced treasury, which is the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle;
third is the medium-priced treasury, which is the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
The fourth is the treasury of the lower price, which is the vehicle of humans and devas.
Furthermore, the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) also constitute the four treasuries.
"Furthermore, Guṇamati" and below refers to the fifth, the Dharma Master.
The threefold explanation of the name:

First, the designation of the stage. This refers to one whose ethical discipline (*śīla*) is pure and who is co-arisen with wisdom (*prajñā*), abiding in the three virtues; therefore, he is named "Virtuous Wisdom" (*Guṇamati*).
"By means of the four immeasurable minds," and so forth, the second section distinguishes the differences in contemplation.
This passage has three parts:
first, it reveals the specific practices of the stages; for the purpose of counteracting afflictions such as hatred, one cultivates the four immeasurables (brahmavihāras).
"Eliminating anger toward the three realms of existence" and below clarifies the removal of hindrances.
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, anger exists only in the desire realm;
according to the *Tattvasiddhi* school, anger pervades all three realms.
According to the "Parable" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there is also anger in the higher [stages].
The phrase "abiding in middle patience" below refers to the boundaries of the three stages.
"Conforming patience" (*anulomikī kṣānti*) is the middle grade.

"Furthermore, 'Vimalaprabhā' (Clear Wisdom)" and below refers to the sixth Dharma-preacher.
The text has three parts:
first, the designation of the stage; because he has attained the perfection of *kṣānti* (patience), he is named Vimalaprabhā.
From "Always by means of the signless" (*nityam animittena*) onwards, the second section distinguishes the contemplation.
This passage has three parts:
first, the explanation of the specific practices of each stage (*bhūmi*).
To know that the three periods of time are empty is the contemplation of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*).

From "attaining the three supernormal knowledges" onwards, the stages of the three supernormal knowledges are fulfilled.
"Constantly by six asaṃkhyeyas," and so forth, [indicates] the temporal duration for entering the stages [of the bodhisattva path].
"Kalāpa" means "crossing the limits"; it refers to crossing over the various limits of the [three] knowledges (vidyā).
"Furthermore, regarding 'objects of cognition' (*jñeya*) below," this is the seventh section on the Dharma Master.
The text has three parts:
first, the heading.
The term *er-yan* (爾焰) is translated here as "mother of wisdom.
This means that within this stage, one can give rise to the wisdom of dhyāna; therefore, it is called the "mother of wisdom.
The section beginning with "cultivating the patience that accords with the Dharma" (*xiūxíng shùn fǎrěn*) clarifies the specific practices of each stage.
The text has three parts:
first, it indicates the stage of abiding.
The term "Srotāpanna" (Stream-enterer) is used here as a designation from the Lesser Vehicle to refer to the Greater Vehicle.
The "five views" refer to the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-kleśāḥ*).
From the passage beginning with "constantly with the divine eye," two supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) arise.
Since he has not yet attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), only these five are mentioned.
From "In every thought-moment" onwards, there are three [sections] on the elimination of hindrances.
This means that since this stage corresponds to the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*) are eliminated.
Furthermore, this also represents the sense of entering the general [path] from the particular.

because he has deeply cultivated meditative concentration (dhyāna), he attains supernormal powers (abhijñā); because he penetrates the phenomena of form and mind, he is called "Supreme Penetration" (visheshagamana).

Section Three:
First, explaining the attainment of the contemplation of fearlessness.
Thoroughly penetrating the five characteristics constitutes the fearlessness of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

first, the designation of the stage.
Because the true illumination of the Middle Way is the reality of *prajñā*, it constantly manifests as the ultimate truth.
"Abiding in the stage of compliance with patience" (住順忍中) and below constitutes the second part: distinct practices.
All afflictions constitute the "cause of accumulation" (集因), while suffering and so forth are termed the "karma of accumulation" (集業); both are completely exhausted within this stage.

Because all dharmas are fundamentally empty, they are not existent; because all dharmas are established, they are not non-existent. Since neither existence nor non-existence is real, they have a single characteristic; since this true characteristic is also suchness, it is without characteristics.
"Furthermore, in the nine *kalpas*" and below, [the text] describes the duration of entering the stages.
"The power of joy" (*rati-bala*) refers to the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-bala*).

The commentary has three parts.
First, the designation of the stage: "Mysterious" (xuán) means remote;
"penetrating" (dá) means pervasive.
In this stage, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) with effortless mental application; hence it is called "profoundly penetrating.
The section beginning with "ten *asaṃkhyeya*" concerns the second point: the temporal duration of entering the stages.
It means to extinguish the habitual afflictions of the three realms.
As for "dwelling in the tenth stage," this refers to the stage of the tenth Dharma Master among the thirteen Dharma Masters, and does not refer to a Bodhisattva of the [Bodhisattva] Ten Stages.
"Constantly practicing the three gates of emptiness" and below, the third section distinguishes the differences in contemplation;
this is because one practices the contemplation of the three emptinesses to propagate the Buddha’s three Dharma-piṭakas.
