The text has three parts;
first, the designation of the stage.

That which is called "Equal Enlightenment" (Samyaksambodhi) within the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), characterized by the simultaneous illumination of both the ultimate and the conventional, is not the Equal Enlightenment of the eleventh stage.
Below the section "Abiding in Non-arising," the second part clarifies the distinctions among contemplations.
This section has three parts;
the first clarifies the contemplation of existence and non-existence, which further consists of two sub-sections:
The preceding section was the preliminary arrangement of positions.
Below the phrase "Contemplating the mind within the mind," there are two parts that correctly distinguish the contemplation of existence and non-existence.
The text is divided into three sections:
First, the individual explanation.
This section has two parts:
first, clarifying that while quiescent, it is constantly active.
"The mind and mind are quiescent" means that every thought-moment is empty; this clarifies the meaning of "quiescence. Although there are no marks, there are marks;
although there is no body, there is a body; although there is no cognition, there is cognition; this clarifies the meaning of "function."
"Furthermore, applying the mind" and below clarifies that while functioning, one is always quiescent.
"While existing, constantly cultivating emptiness" and below provides a combined explanation of existence and non-existence.
"While existing, cultivating emptiness" explains how, while functioning, one is always quiescent.
"Abiding in emptiness while constantly manifesting the myriad transformations" explains that while [the mind] is quiescent, it is nevertheless functionally active.
"Because it illuminates all phenomena simultaneously" constitutes the third pair of conclusions.
"Knowing what is possible and what is impossible" and below, the second section clarifies the contemplation of the ten powers (*daśabala*).
Only the final one is explicitly explained, while the remaining practices are abbreviated.
"Thereby ascending to the stage of Mahāraga and transforming sentient beings in all lands" constitutes the third [section]: the distinctions regarding the ascent to the stage.
“Mahoraga” is translated here as “Great Attainer,” or alternatively as “Dragon-Elephant.
The phrase “a thousand asaṃkhyeyas” below indicates the duration of time for the practice of the three types of supernormal knowledge (vidyā).
"Furthermore, 'Wisdom Light' (Hui-guang)" and below is the twelfth [section], the Dharma Master.
The text has three parts:

first, the designation of the stage. Because the Bodhisattvas of this stage attain unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna*), they transform all sentient beings and manifest various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); thus it is called "The Supernatural Transformation of Wisdom Light."
"Abiding in the highest of the high": the following section clarifies the distinctions between contemplations.
This text consists of four parts;
first is the assignment of stages.

Regarding "extinguishing the mind and its mental characteristics": first, it clarifies that extinguishing the mind and extinguishing the intellect (*manas*) and so forth is called "extinguishing the mind," while extinguishing the mental factors (*caitasika*) is called "extinguishing the characteristics.
From the phrase "seeing with the Dharma-eye" onward, it thirdly clarifies the perception of objects.
The Dharma-eye perceives all phenomena; this clarifies them individually.
The three eyes perceive that form is empty; this clarifies them collectively.
As for the three eyes, they are the Buddha-eye, the Dharma-eye, and the Wisdom-eye.
The wisdom-eye sees that form is empty; the dharma-eye sees that form is provisional; the buddha-eye sees the Middle Way.
Emptiness and provisionality are non-dual yet dual, and dual yet non-dual.
When both are illuminated, it is non-duality appearing as duality; when both are forgotten, it is duality being non-duality.
By citing the three eyes in relation to the two objects of form, the single character "seeing" (jìan) comprehensively clarifies the distinctions among the three types of vision.

Seeing that form is empty is the Truth of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-satya*); seeing that form is provisional is the Truth of Existence (*saṃvṛti-satya*); illuminating both simultaneously is the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Regarding these three truths according to the teachings, there are five [applications]:
first, the separate entry into the universal, wherein illusory form is taken as existence, seeing emptiness as the real, and that which is neither existence nor emptiness is the Ultimate Truth.
Second, the Perfect Entry into the Common [Teaching]: the three truths are the same as before, with the addition of "all dharmas tending toward" [the truth].
Third, the Separate Teaching: it takes the illusory existence that is identical to emptiness as the conventional, non-emptiness as the true, and neither existence nor non-existence as the Middle Way.
The fourth [classification] distinguishes the four perfect entrances (*pariniṣpanna-praveśa*), adding "all dharmas proceed toward" (*sarva-dharma-yānti*) to the middle [truth].
The fifth is the Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa-śāsana*), wherein all three truths are stated as "all dharmas proceed toward.
Question:
Question: Why is it said that the Bodhisattva-bhūmi possesses the Buddha-eye? Answer:

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states, "Opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This refers to the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching and the first dwelling (*vihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching, wherein one gives rise to the three kinds of wisdom: [the wisdom of the path, the wisdom of phenomena, and the wisdom of non-arising].
First, the mind of the causal principle of the primary cause arises, employing the contemplation of the Middle Way to open the gate of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Second, the mind of the causal principle of knowledge arises, employing the contemplation of immediate emptiness to open the gate of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Third, when a wholesome mind arises through causal conditions, the provisional contemplation is employed to open the Path Wisdom (*mārgajñatā*).
If this is already attained even at the first stage (*bhūmi*), how much more so at the ninth?
This is merely a partial attainment, not a complete one.
The section beginning with "By the power of great vows" describes the purification of the four modes of birth in the Pure Land.
The section beginning with "Ten thousand asaṃkhyeyas" clarifies the duration of time for entering the stage [of Buddhahood].
"Bhagavān" is translated here as "World-Honored One"; this is not the true Buddha-World-Honored One, but rather the World-Honored One of the Stage of Rebirth (the Bodhisattva of the Final Birth).
"Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas," and so forth, is the thirteenth section on the Dharma Master.
The text has four parts:
first, the designation of the stage.

Regarding "Contemplating the Buddha and Bodhisattvas": if one opens the wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), this refers to the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samanvāgama-bhūmi*), which is still called a bodhisattva; having reached this stage, one maintains it as the ultimate, yet as it is not yet the final limit, one must continue to observe.
In the case of a distinct Buddha, there remain thirty-two grades of ignorance; since wisdom is still far from perfect Buddhahood, it is called "contemplation.
In the case of a Universal Buddha, there are forty-two grades of ignorance, which is even further away.
Below the section "Abiding in the Patience of Quiescence," the second part clarifies the timing of realization.
This consists of four sections;
first, the correlation with the stages: within the fifth stage, the patience of quiescence itself, there are two distinct divisions.
One descent and two ascents.
The present tenth stage is precisely the lower grade of the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānti-kṣānti*).
The passage beginning with "From the initial generation of the mind" below [indicates] the second [point]: the duration of time.
This refers to the period from the stage of the nature of practice (*śikṣāgotra*) up to the patience of consecration (*abhiṣeka-kṣānti*), spanning one million *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Following the phrase "cultivating for one million," the third section distinguishes the cultivation and realization.
Below the phrase "ascending all dharmas," the fourth section clarifies the stage of ascent.
"Liberation from all dharmas" refers to true liberation.
"Vajra Terrace" is the Vajra Samādhi.
"Good son," and so forth, below, distinguishes the three pairs of stages.
The text has five parts:

first, the distinction between suppression and abandonment; from the stage of practice (*śikṣā*) up to the summit of concentration (*mūrdhan-samādhi*), it first clarifies the patience of suppression (*vinaya-kṣānti*).
The phrase "and there is no mutual trust" below clarifies the severance [of afflictions].
"Extinguishing all afflictions" is Great Nirvana;
"giving rise to liberation" is the wisdom of liberation.
“Illumination” is *prajñā*.
“The Ultimate Truth” (*paramārtha*) is the stage of the *dharmakāya*.
The section beginning with “is not called seeing” distinguishes between the two types of faith and seeing.
First, "not seeing" is clarified:
"That which is called 'seeing' is omniscience (*sarvajñā*)"; next, "seeing" is clarified:
"Therefore, from the past until now," and so forth, which serves as a scriptural citation.
"Only the Buddha understands instantaneously" marks the third [point], the distinction between the gradual and the instantaneous.
"Although wisdom arises and ceases" marks the fourth, the difference between the permanent and the impermanent.
When there is no arising, all afflictions are eliminated; when there is no ceasing, all virtues are perfected.
Non-arising is the virtue of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*), and non-extinction is the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "Entering the exhaustion of principle," the five grades and their distinctions from the peerless are explained through the three sections of the text:
the teaching (*dharma*), the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*upanaya*), which are readily understandable.
"Constantly cultivating all" and below clarify the stage of entering the state of certainty.
Herein, the fulfillment of all practices and the fulfillment of wisdom is called the "Treasury of Merit."
"Bhagavat" is translated here as "World-Honored One.
Regarding the phrase "also constantly abiding in the Buddha-wisdom samādhi," the word "also" (亦復) implies that one must necessarily undergo cultivation and practice.
Because he benefits others in other realms, it is said that he is "eternally abiding.
From the passage beginning "Good son, in this way," the third major section concludes with a praise, clarifying that his manifestation of transformation is no different from that of the Buddha.
From "The Buddha addressed King Prasenajit" onwards is the second section, Entrusting the King to Uphold [the Teaching].
This passage has four parts:

first, praising its function to encourage upholding; second, praising its name to encourage upholding; third, explaining the reason for the exhortation; and fourth, calling out the name to entrust it.
The first section has two parts:
first, a brief praise; second, an extensive praise.
The first part further consists of four sections:
The first section, "In one stroke, they are extinguished," exhorts [the audience] to uphold [the teaching]. The section beginning with "All lands" clarifies the power of Prajñā.
The section beginning with "Therefore, the entrustment" explains the reason for the entrustment.
"Because he lacks the sovereign power of a king, he is not entrusted [with this teaching].
The section beginning with "You should receive and uphold it" below constitutes the fourth part, which specifically entrusts [the teaching] to Candraprabha.
The section beginning with "Great King, those whom I have now converted" below is the second part, which extensively praises [the recipient] and exhorts him to uphold [the teaching].
The text has two parts:
first, the statement that merit arises through the removal of difficulties; second, the detailed analysis through questions and answers.
Regarding the first part now, the text is easily understood.
Regarding the section beginning with "What are the seven calamities?", there are two parts: the question-and-answer analysis.
First is the question, which is easily understood.
Following the phrase "The sun and moon lose their courses," there are two answers.
The seven calamities are as follows:

first, the calamity of the sun and moon losing their proper courses, which means that when the seasons change irregularly, there is much famine; when quantities [of time] change irregularly, there is much warfare; and when physical appearances change irregularly, there is much pestilence.
"Twenty-eight" below refers to the difficulty of the two lunar mansions losing their proper course.
"A great fire burns the country" below refers to the difficulty of the calamity of fire.
"Great waters flood and submerge [the land]" below refers to the difficulty of the transformation of rainwater.
"Great winds blow and kill ten thousand people" refers below to the calamity of the five evil winds.
"Heaven, earth, and the land" refers below to the sixth calamity of excessive drought.
"From 'The enemies come from the four directions' onwards, there is the difficulty of the seven evil thieves;
all is as can be seen in the text.
From 'Great King, this is Prajñā' onwards, it is the second section: praising the name and exhorting its upholding."
The text has two parts:
first, praising its name as supreme; second, exhorting one to make offerings.
Within the first part, the three types of *prajñā* are distinguished.
"The root of mind-consciousness" is the *prajñā* of the true nature (*dharmatā*);
"the parents of the king" is the *prajñā* of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), because it can give birth to the king’s wisdom and understanding;
the six subsequent names are the *prajñā* of words and letters (*vyañjana*).
From "The Buddha said to the Great King" onwards, there are two sections encouraging offerings.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, showing the method of making offerings; second, specifically clarifying the offerings made while walking and staying.

The reason both the beginning and the middle state that there are nine is that the number nine symbolizes the suffering of sentient beings; "banners" (fan) signify the manifestation of attaining excellence through practice, clarifying that within the midst of the nine sufferings, one erects the banner of victory of liberation.
The "nine-colored flowers" represent the practice of the nine types of suffering sentient beings as the cause for *prajñā*.

The five-colored flowers—blue, yellow, red, white, and black—are the flowers of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*); the [remaining] four colors are the flowers of the four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*: earth, water, fire, and wind).

The "two zhang" symbolize the two truths, and the "ten lamps" symbolize the ten meritorious virtues of good conduct; each, through the mutual support of *prajñā*, gives rise to the wisdom of a thousand Buddhas.
"Five zhang in height" signifies the illuminating light that shines throughout the five realms of existence.
"Nine jade caskets" symbolize that those dwelling in the nine abodes of suffering are pure and serve as vessels for the Dharma.
"Nine jade cloths" symbolize that sentient beings dwelling in the nine abodes of suffering obtain the cloth of Prajñā.
"Tablet" (an) signifies levelness, serving as a metaphor for the *prajñā* of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
"Placing the sutra upon it" means that written words can cause the true principle to become manifest.
"The seven treasures" represent the people of the seven skillful means (*upāya*), all of whom are jewels among men.
From "When the king travels" onwards, there are two sections specifically clarifying the offerings made while traveling and while staying; first, the offerings made while traveling are explained.
From "When the king stays" onwards, this explains the offerings made while staying.
"Great King, I now possess the five eyes," and so forth; this section provides three explanations for the reasons behind the exhortation.
The text has two parts:
first, it clarifies that the King’s merit is exhausted, which is easily understood.
"Great King, if in future ages... and so forth, the second section clarifies the benefits for future lives.
This passage has three parts;
the first, which enumerates the number [of benefits], is easily understood.
From "The Bodhisattva Vajragarjita" onwards is the second section, the individual explanations, which may be understood as they appear.
From "These five great beings" onwards is the third section, the concluding explanation.
"Great King, I now [entrust] the Three Jewels," and so forth, constitutes the fourth section: the entrustment by name.
This passage has three parts;
the first, which provides a general explanation of the entrustment, is easily understood.
Below "the kingdom of Kośala," there is the second [section], which names [the location].
Below "all such as these," there is the third [section], which concludes with an exhortation.
Below "at that time, the great assembly," there is the third [part], concerning the benefits gained by the assembly at that time.
Section Five:
First, the benefit for the asuras;
from "At that time, the sixteen... onwards, the benefit for the two human kings.
In the first section of this [chapter on] benefits, the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are explained.
Earth, water, fire, and wind are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) capable of creating; blue, yellow, red, and white are the derivative forms (*upādāyarūpa*) created by them.
Because one departs from desire, they are called "mastery" (*abhibhava*).

Following the "Four Great Elements" (*mahābhūta*), the ten spheres of totality (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*) are next explained: earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, white, the sphere of infinite space, and the sphere of infinite consciousness.
These are so called because their objects of perception are realized as vast, penetrating everywhere without exception.
The "thirty patiences" are the skillful means of the first stage and are termed the "characteristics of the first stage.
The "ultimate truth" (paramārtha-satya) is itself the first stage; the first stage is the characteristic of all nine stages.
Therefore, a verse in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Just as when the first knot of a bamboo is split, the remaining knots can quickly be split;
having attained the true wisdom of the first stage, the other stages will swiftly be accomplished."

One abandons the ordinary body to attain the body of the sixth stage; one abandons the retributive body of segmented existence of the seventh stage to attain the transformational dharma-body of the eighth stage.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the seventh [stage], one abandons the birth-body and the fleshly body. This is the benefit of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*).
Below "the eighteen Brahma heavens," the three heavens receive further benefit; the asuras and devas all likewise receive this benefit.

"Flowers in the sky" symbolizes the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), while "flowers of the dharma-nature" symbolizes the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); this reveals the patience of subduing (*kṣānti*).

The "Flower of the Noble Ones" (ārya-puṣpa) symbolizes the patience of conviction (adhimukti-kṣānti); the "Conforming Flower" (anuloma-puṣpa) symbolizes the conforming patience (anuloma-kṣānti); and the "Unarisen Flower" (anutpāda-puṣpa) symbolizes the patience of non-arising (anutpāda-kṣānti).

The preaching of the Dharma with mastery over the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) is the "Flower of Dharma-Bliss," which corresponds to the lower grade of the patience of cessation (śānti-kṣānti).
The Vajrasamādhi can sever the fetters and afflictions; it is precisely the patience of quiescence of a single grade.
The passage "the rest of all the assemblies" below concerns the benefits for the four great assemblies.
"Mind as a flower in the sky" refers to the training of the mind (citta-śikṣā) among the three trainings.
"Flowers on the tree of the mind" refers to contemplating the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination.
"The Flower of the Six Perfections" refers to the practice of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
"The Flower of Wondrous Enlightenment" refers to the practice of the fruition.
From "the ten thousand bodhisattvas" downward, these are the names of five bodhisattvas.
The commentary has two parts:
first, the benefit of ten thousand [beings] is clear and can be understood.
Second, from "Furthermore, there are ten billion" onwards, it clarifies the benefit of attaining Buddhahood.
This section establishes the Buddha of the Distinct Teaching.
Chapter Eight: Entrustment (The Third Major Section of the Circulation Portion). “Entrust” (*zhù*) means to hand over;
“cumulatively” (*lèi*) means to rely upon. Because this Dharma is handed over to kings and entrusted to them to propagate and expound it, it is called the “Chapter on Entrustment.”
Furthermore, it is entrusted to the king so that, should any calamities arise, he may rely upon this for deliverance; hence it is called "Entrustment" (*parindanā*).
Moreover, because this sutra is entrusted [to him] so that it may circulate through successive generations, it is named the "Chapter on Entrustment."
Question:

Why is it that, unlike the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* which entrusts [the teaching] to the śrāvakas and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* which entrusts it to the bodhisattvas, this one instead entrusts it to the king?
Answer:
This Buddha administers medicine according to the illness.
He entrusts [the teaching] because it will bring great benefit through its widespread proclamation during times of calamity within the kingdom.
Furthermore, these hundredfold great offerings are profound and vast; were it not for the power of the king, who else could have accomplished them?
Therefore, he entrusts [the Dharma] to him.
Moreover, if the king does not believe, the Dharma will not be practiced.
"The practice of the Dharma rests with the king; therefore, it is entrusted to him.
From "The Buddha addressed King Prasenajit" onwards, the text is divided into two parts:
first, the entrustment and admonition; second, the reverent upholding according to the teaching.
The first part consists of two sections:
first, the brief entrustment.
"Jie" (誡) means admonition and exhortation; "chi" (勅) means instruction and command.
"From 'After my parinirvāṇa' onwards, there are two sections: first, the extensive entrustment, and second, the admonition.
The initial text has two parts:
first, the clarification of the entrustment; second, the clarification of the admonition."
Regarding the first and second [sections]:
first, the time of entrustment; second, the actual clarification of the method for entrusting persons.
This is the first.
Regarding the phrase "eighty years": within the hundred years after the Buddha’s passing, five individuals maintained the teachings:

first Kāśyapa, second Ānanda, and third Madhyāntika. These three had seen the Buddha while he was alive; they maintained the teachings in succession, and for sixty years the practice of the Dharma did not perish.

Next came Śaṇavāsa and Upagupta; these two did not see the Buddha, yet they successively maintained the teachings for forty years until the majestic deportment and the Dharma were extinguished. Therefore, it is said that at this time there was no Buddha, Dharma, or Saṅgha.
Regarding the statement "eight hundred years," within the years of the True Dharma (Saddharma), twenty masters will uphold the Buddha-dharma, all of whom are sages, and the Dharma shall not perish.
In the sixth century, the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa; in the seventh century, Nāgārjuna—both were bodhisattvas, and the Dharma likewise did not perish.

During the eight hundred years when heterodox teachings flourished to the utmost, it was at this time that he entrusted [the Dharma] to the king; it was Deva Bodhisattva who beat the drum of King Śrī and proclaimed the Dharma.

Regarding the "eight thousand years": this refers to the period when the Semblance Dharma has ended and the Final Dharma prevails; because sentient beings believe in heterodoxies, the Dharma is extinguished.
From the phrase "the Three Jewels of this sutra" onwards, the second section clarifies the entrustment of the person and the Dharma.
There are two further points:
the first, the entrustment of the Dharma, is easily understood.
From "For the sake of sentient beings of the three realms" onwards, is the second, the entrustment to persons.
Now I shall teach three types of practice: first, the practice of emptiness; second, the practice of the seven worthies; and third, the practice of the ten wholesome deeds.
Emptiness is the noble practice; the seven worthies are the seven expedient means; and the ten wholesome deeds are the practices of ordinary beings. These proceed from the profound to the shallow.
From "In the future age of the five turbidities" onwards is the second section, which extensively explains the seven admonitions.

The text consists of seven parts: first, an admonition against the faults of extinguishing the Dharma; second, an admonition against destroying the practices of the fourfold assembly; third, an admonition against not relying on the Dharma; fourth, an admonition against self-destruction; fifth, an admonition against exploitation; sixth, an admonition against self-reproach; and seventh, an admonition against false faith.
Now, first, the initial admonition regarding the faults of those who destroy the Dharma.
The text has three parts:
first, clarifying the person who destroys the Dharma; second, distinguishing the faults of destroying the Dharma; and third, concluding by establishing these faults.
The first section of the initial text has two parts:

first, it clarifies the period when the Dharma is extinguished, which refers to the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*): first, the turbidity of life; second, the turbidity of the eon; third, the turbidity of afflictions; fourth, the turbidity of views; and fifth, the turbidity of sentient beings.

The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: "Lifespan ranging from ten years up to a thousand years constitutes the defilement of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*). Famine, exhaustion, disease, and warfare constitute the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). The abundance of greed, hatred, and delusion is called the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). False views, attachment to precepts and rituals, attachment to views, and extreme views constitute the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Lack of filial piety, lack of righteousness, and disparaging one's teachers and elders are the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*)."
"Below 'Bhikṣu,' there are two points concerning those who cause the Dharma to perish.
Below 'Clearly Establishing the Regulative Dharma,' there are two points distinguishing the faults of causing the Dharma to perish.
Within the text, it first clarifies the establishment of the four correct [practices] and subsequently clarifies the setting forth of the four deviant [practices]."

The four prohibitions are: first, not permitting ordination; second, not permitting the practice of the Path; third, not permitting the making of images; and fourth, not permitting the construction of stupas. The four heterodox practices established are:

first, establishing a central authority to control the assembly; second, allowing laypeople to occupy high seats on monastic grounds while bhikṣus remain standing; third, allowing soldiers and slaves to become bhikṣus; and fourth, accepting separate invitations for meals.
The section beginning with "You should know that at that time" concludes the third point regarding the transgressions.

The section beginning with "The Great King has brought disorder to my Way" constitutes the second point, which is a warning against the destruction of the conduct of the fourfold assembly; it teaches that if a king does not practice the True Dharma, the Buddha-way will be ruined.
"O Great King, in the final age of the Dharma," and so forth, constitutes the third admonition: not to rely on the Dharma.
"O Great King, after my parinirvāṇa," and so forth, constitutes the fourth admonition: not to bring oneself to ruin.
The prose section has three parts:
first, self-destruction; second, the arising of evil; and third, the invitation of retribution.
The first part has two sections:
First the principle, then the analogy.
Now, for the first part, the text is clear.
From "Like the body of a lion" onwards, the second part clarifies the analogy, which is as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-mukha-sūtra*: "The Buddha told Ānanda:"
"For example, when a lion dies and its life ends, no sentient beings—whether in the air, on the earth, in the water, or on land—dare to eat its flesh.
Only the various worms born from the lion's own body consume the lion's flesh."
"Ānanda!
In my Buddha-dharma, it is not others who cause destruction; rather, this bhikṣu destroys my Dharma of three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
While that sutra uses this as a metaphor specifically for those who have left the household life, this sutra applies the metaphor universally to both monastics and laypeople.
"Each one destroys my Buddha-dharma" marks the second section, the arising of evil.
"People destroy the Buddhist teaching" marks the third section, the retribution incurred.
Within the text, the Dharma, the analogy, and the application can be clearly discerned.
The "six relatives" refer to parents, siblings, and spouses.
There are three metaphors:
the first two illustrate retribution in the present life, while the last one illustrates retribution in future lives.
"O Great King, in future ages," and so forth, constitutes the fifth admonition regarding the commissioning of labor.
"O Great King, in future ages," and so forth, constitutes the sixth admonition regarding self-reproach.
"Great King, in future ages," and so forth, [the text] below provides seven admonitions against erroneous faith.
The passage is divided into four parts;
first, it demonstrates what is wholesome.
"Not undermining the true teaching" is called "flowing"; "opening the path of the dharma of emptiness" is called "penetrating"; and "being able to contain merit and wisdom" is called a "vessel.
From the phrase "various evil bhikṣus" onwards, the second section demonstrates their wickedness.
"His king did not distinguish [the true from the false]" and below is the third section on deluded faith.
"This constitutes a destruction of the Buddha's [teaching]" and below is the fourth section showing the faults.
"At that time, the sixteen kings... and below is the second section on the great assembly upholding [the teaching].
The text has two parts:
first, receiving and upholding; second, practicing accordingly.
In the first part, there are two sections: first, expressing sorrow and emotion; second, uttering praise.
The first section has two parts:
first, the explicit explanation of the expression of grief;
second, from "At that time, the various kings and others... onwards, the acceptance and upholding [of the teaching].
From "At that time, the great assembly" onwards, there are two sections on lamentation, expressing grief for this period.
From "At that time, among the immeasurable great assembly" onwards, there are two sections on the practice and observance.
Section Five:
First, the assembly is enumerated.
From "Hearing what the Buddha has taught" onwards, second, the meaning of hearing the Buddha’s Dharma is elucidated.
"Rejoicing immeasurably" refers to the third [step], rejoicing.
"Prostrating to the Buddha" refers to the fourth, prostrating to the Buddha.
"Receiving and upholding the Prajñāpāramitā" refers to the fifth, practicing in accordance with the teaching.
